A field treatise for fixed charge receivers, the lenders who appoint them, and their advisers · X

How Fixed Charge Receivers use Reflective Practice

Donald Schön’s reflection-in-action (thinking as you go) and reflection-on-action (looking back after the fact), the tacit knowledge it rests on (Polanyi, Ryle, Collins, Dreyfus, Klein), knowledge creation and its critics (Nonaka and Takeuchi’s SECI, Tsoukas, Gourlay, Stacey, Snowden’s ASHEN), cognitive mapping (Tolman, Kelly, Axelrod, Eden and Ackermann, Kosko), risk, spontaneity and improvisation (Schön’s jazz, Weick, Barrett, Johnstone, Mann Gulch, Shaw and Stacey’s “working live”), process thinking (Chia and Tsoukas) and sensemaking (Weick’s 2020 handoff), the long tradition of reflective practice from Dewey to Mezirow, and the after action review from the US Army’s National Training Center to Tom Graves’s extended xAAR, brought to one appointment: a half-converted tower block, forty-two tenant households and a lender who wants a date

Receivers are paid for judgement. Most of that judgement is exercised on the move, in situations no textbook describes, and most of it is never examined afterwards. This treatise is about how a receiver can think well while acting, look back honestly once the action is over, surface and map the tacit knowledge his judgement rests on, act and improvise under risk without losing the people around him, and turn all of it into learning that is recorded and owned. The receiver’s own learning and the team’s shared learning are recorded separately, because they are separate commitments.

Mark Downham
BA (Hons) MPhil MBA FRICS FNARA RPR · LPA and Fixed Charge Receiver since 1989 · more than 1,000 appointments · workout strategist, complexity thinker and game theory practitioner

01 · The field

Ferrier House: an appointment in the swamp

In brief

This treatise follows one composite appointment over a seven-storey 1960s office block, part-converted into sixty-four flats. Forty-two flats are finished and let; twenty-two are shells. The contractor has failed, the borrower has defaulted, and nothing about the building matches the file. It is an appointment in which almost every important decision has to be made before the facts are in, which is exactly the condition Schön wrote about.

Ferrier House stands on the ring road of a Midlands city. It was built in 1968 as offices for an insurance company, emptied in the 2010s, and bought in 2021 by a single-purpose company that set out to convert it into sixty-four flats. A development lender advanced £6.1 million against the conversion. In 2024 the main contractor went into administration with floors one to five finished and floors six and seven stripped to the frame. The borrower let the forty-two finished flats on assured shorthold tenancies through a local letting agent, used the rent to service part of the interest for a year, and then stopped paying anything. The lender appoints a fixed charge receiver on a Thursday in late October.

The file describes a building that is “substantially complete, 66 per cent let, with modest finishing works outstanding”. The receiver’s first walk-round on the Friday describes a different building. The upper floors are open to the weather where a contractor’s temporary sheeting has blown away. The fire doors on the stair landings of floors five to seven are missing their closers. A tenant on the fourth floor, a nurse who works nights, stops him in the corridor to say that her son’s bedroom has black mould behind the wardrobe and that the agent has not answered for six weeks. The agent’s office, when he rings it, cannot say with certainty which tenants’ deposits have been protected.

None of this is unusual. Every experienced receiver has walked into a building whose file was written for a credit committee rather than for the person who has to run it. What matters for this treatise is what the receiver does with the gap between the file and the building. He can treat it as noise: apply his standard first-week checklist and let the surprises be handled as they come. Or he can treat the gap as information: a signal that his own model of the appointment is already wrong, and that the next few days will be spent finding out how.

The high ground and the swamp

Schön’s best-known image, from the second chapter of The Reflective Practitioner, is a landscape. There is a high, hard ground where research-based theory and technique work, and a swampy lowland of confusing “messes” that resist technical solution. The trouble, he says, is that the high-ground problems are often relatively unimportant to clients, while the problems of greatest human concern lie in the swamp. The fourth-floor bedroom at Ferrier House is in the swamp. So is the question of whether to complete the upper floors or sell the building as it stands.

The appointment runs for eleven months. The treatise follows it through six moments of surprise, each of which calls for a different kind of reflection, and ends with the review the lender, the receiver and the managing agent hold together once the sale completes. That review is built on Graves’s extended After Action Review. It records two kinds of learning separately: what each person will do differently, and what the three of them will do differently as a team.

Why this matters for a receiver

The lender pays the receiver for judgement under uncertainty. Judgement that is never examined does not improve; it hardens. Schön called this “over-learning”: a practitioner who sees the same kinds of case for years becomes less and less open to surprise, and starts to miss what does not fit his categories. Reflective practice is the discipline that keeps a receiver’s judgement alive.

Key terms
Reflection-in-action
Thinking about what one is doing while doing it, within the time in which thinking can still change the outcome.
Reflection-on-action
Thinking back over action after the fact, to understand it and learn from it.
After Action Review (AAR)
A structured, non-punitive team discussion comparing what was supposed to happen with what did, and why.
Ferrier House
This treatise’s composite worked case. Its people and numbers are invented for illustration.

02 · The source

Schön and the crisis of professional knowledge

In brief

Schön wrote The Reflective Practitioner to challenge what he called Technical Rationality: the view that professional practice is the application of scientific theory to well-formed problems. He argued that real practice begins earlier, in problem setting, and that competent practitioners know more than they can say. A receivership is a case in point.

Donald Schön (1930–1997) was a philosopher who worked as an industrial consultant, technology manager, planner and policy analyst before teaching urban studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. His preface explains that the question of the relationship between academic knowledge and practical competence had become, for him, a personal quest. The book that came out of it, published in 1983, examines what architects, psychotherapists, engineers, planners and managers actually do, and builds from those vignettes an alternative “epistemology of practice”.

His target is a model he calls Technical Rationality, which he traces to nineteenth-century Positivism. On this view professional activity is instrumental problem solving, made rigorous by applying scientific theory and technique. Knowledge forms a hierarchy: basic science at the top, applied science beneath it, and at the bottom the “skills” of applying it, which are hardly counted as knowledge at all. The professional school mirrors the hierarchy: science first, practicum later.

Schön’s objection is that this model has nothing to say about the most important part of practice. Problems, he writes, do not present themselves to the practitioner as givens. They must be constructed from the materials of situations that are puzzling, troubling and uncertain. Technical Rationality concentrates on problem solving and ignores problem setting: the process by which we define the decision to be made, the ends to be achieved and the means that may be chosen. Once a problem is well set, technique may solve it. Setting it is not a technical act.

The banker who could calculate a quarter of the risk

One of Schön’s brief examples could have been written for this series. An investment banker tells him that the ordinary rules of thumb let him calculate only “20 to 30 percent” of the risk in an investment. A company’s numbers may be excellent; but if management’s explanation does not fit the numbers, or something is odd in how people behave, that is a worry to be considered afresh each time. He recalls a day with a large Latin American bank whose figures were satisfactory, and a gnawing feeling that something was wrong. He realised it was the deference he had been shown, out of all proportion to his standing. He told his colleague: no new business with them. Months later the bank failed, and there had been nothing wrong with the numbers.

Lenders and receivers live in that remaining 70 to 80 per cent. The valuation, the rent roll and the covenant tests are the high ground. The borrower’s silence, the agent’s evasiveness, the way a tenant says “they never answer” are the swamp, and they are often where the real risk lies.

Why this matters for a receiver

A receiver is appointed after Technical Rationality has failed. The lender’s models said the loan was sound. The receiver’s first job is problem setting: working out what kind of problem this building actually is. That cannot be done from the file.

Key terms
Technical Rationality
Schön’s name for the view that professional practice is the application of scientific theory and technique to instrumental problems.
Problem setting
Constructing the problem from an uncertain situation: naming what to attend to and framing the context in which to attend to it.
Epistemology of practice
An account of the kind of knowing competent practitioners display, which Schön sought as an alternative to Technical Rationality.
Cards · Schön
03 · The tacit

Knowing-in-action: what a receiver knows and cannot say

In brief

Most of what a competent practitioner knows is tacit: it is in the doing, not in any rule the practitioner could state. Schön calls it knowing-in-action. It is the source of a receiver’s speed and reliability. It is also the source of his blind spots, because tacit knowing that is never examined turns into what Schön called over-learning.

Schön begins from ordinary competence. When we ride a bicycle, catch a ball or recognise a face, we show that we know something, and when we try to describe it we either cannot or produce descriptions that are plainly inadequate. The know-how is in the action. A tightrope walker’s knowledge is revealed in how he crosses the wire; a pitcher’s, in how he pitches to a batter’s weakness. Professionals are no different. Every competent practitioner, Schön says, recognises families of phenomena for which he cannot give an accurate description, makes judgements of quality for which he cannot state the criteria, and displays skills whose rules he cannot set out.

A receiver’s knowing-in-action is easy to list and hard to explain. He knows within a minute of entering a building whether it is being managed. He knows from the tone of a borrower’s first email whether the borrower will cooperate. He knows which agent’s rent roll to trust and which to have checked. He knows when a valuer’s number is a number and when it is a hope. Asked how he knows, he will usually say “experience”, which is true and not an explanation.

Over-learning and selective inattention

The same tacit knowing becomes a hazard as practice settles into routine. Schön describes it carefully. As a practitioner meets many variations on a small number of types of case, he develops a repertoire of expectations, images and techniques, and becomes less and less subject to surprise. That is the benefit of specialisation. The cost is that, as knowing becomes more tacit and automatic, the practitioner may miss chances to think about what he is doing, may be drawn into patterns of error he cannot correct, and may learn to be selectively inattentive to whatever does not fit his categories. When that happens, Schön says, the practitioner has “over-learned” what he knows.

Ferrier House tests this. The receiver’s repertoire for residential blocks with tenants is strong: rent collection, deposit compliance, gas safety, repairs, sale. It is a repertoire for finished buildings. Ferrier House is half a building and half a construction site, and the categories that serve him well on floors one to five will make him inattentive to floors six and seven. The first week is a contest between his repertoire and the building.

Why this matters for a receiver

Senior receivers have the most knowing-in-action and the greatest exposure to over-learning. Schön’s remedy is not to distrust experience but to keep surfacing it: to notice when a judgement was made quickly and ask, later, what it rested on.

Key terms
Knowing-in-action
The tacit, spontaneous knowledge displayed in skilful action.
Repertoire
The stock of examples, images, understandings and actions a practitioner brings to a new situation.
Over-learning
The rigidity that follows when tacit knowing becomes so automatic that it is no longer examined.
Selective inattention
Failing to notice what does not fit one’s existing categories.
Cards · Knowing-in-action
04 · The tacit dimension

Tacit knowledge: what a receiver relies on and cannot fully say

In brief

Schön’s knowing-in-action rests on a longer tradition of thought about tacit knowledge. Michael Polanyi argued that all knowing has a tacit structure: we attend from clues we are only subsidiarily aware of to a whole we are focally aware of. Gilbert Ryle distinguished knowing how from knowing that. Harry Collins split tacit knowledge into three kinds (relational, somatic and collective) which behave very differently when one tries to pass them on. Each distinction changes what reflection can and cannot do for a receiver, and what a review can and cannot capture.

Polanyi: from the clues to the whole

Polanyi’s phrase is famous: we can know more than we can tell. His argument behind it is less well known and more useful. In his 1962 lecture Tacit Knowing he distinguished two kinds of awareness. Focal awareness is knowing a thing by attending to it. Subsidiary awareness is knowing a thing by relying on it in order to attend to something else. When we use a hammer, we are focally aware of the nail and subsidiarily aware of the feel of the handle in the palm. Polanyi called the clues the proximal term of tacit knowing and the whole they reveal the distal term, and he described knowing as a “from–to” relation: we attend from the proximal to the distal. Knowing is tacit, he wrote, to the extent that it has this structure, and he argued that all knowing ultimately does.

Two consequences matter for receivers. First, attending to the clues destroys the whole: if a pianist attends to his fingers he falters. A receiver who tries, in the moment, to list every cue behind his sense that a building is unmanaged will lose the sense. That is why reflection-in-action works through the situation rather than through introspection, and why the cues are better recovered afterwards. Second, Polanyi described skilled perception as indwelling: the experienced practitioner “dwells in” his tools and clues as he dwells in his own body. The probe (the blind man’s stick is Polanyi’s example) becomes an extension of the hand. A receiver’s walk-round, his rent roll and his questions to the agent are probes in this sense. He feels the building through them.

Ryle: knowing how and knowing that

Gilbert Ryle’s The Concept of Mind (1949) attacked what he called the “intellectualist legend”: the view that every intelligent performance is preceded by a private act of consulting a rule. If that were so, Ryle argued, applying the rule would itself need a further rule, and so on without end. Intelligent practice is a matter of knowing how, which is shown in the doing and is not reducible to knowing that. A receiver knows that unprotected deposits create a statutory exposure; he knows how to raise the question with an evasive agent so that the answer comes back true. The first can be written in a manual; the second is learned in practice. Contemporary philosophers still argue about whether knowing how is a kind of knowing that. For practice the distinction remains useful.

Collins: three kinds of tacit knowledge

Harry Collins, in Tacit and Explicit Knowledge (2010), argued that Polanyi’s single term covered three different things. Relational tacit knowledge is tacit for contingent reasons: nobody has written it down, or it is kept secret, or it is too long to tell, or the person does not know what the other needs to know. It could in principle be made explicit. Somatic tacit knowledge lives in bodies and brains (balancing on a bicycle is his example). It can in principle be described, though the describing does not confer the ability. Collective tacit knowledge lives in society: knowing how to apply rules in a social setting, such as knowing how to ride a bicycle through traffic rather than merely how to balance. Collins argued that it cannot currently be made explicit at all, and can be acquired only by being socialised into the relevant community.

The three behave very differently in a review. Relational tacit knowledge is the review’s best harvest: the agent’s former manager’s spreadsheet, the receiver’s unspoken rule of thumb about which valuers round up. Somatic tacit knowledge (the receiver’s feel for a damp building, the smell that says the risers are wet) can be pointed at but not transferred by writing; it passes on walk-rounds. Collective tacit knowledge (knowing how far a particular lender will tolerate a change of strategy, how candid a credit committee can be told to expect a report to be) lives in the lender–receiver–agent relationship itself, and is learned only by working within it. That is one more reason the we ledger is not the I ledger written larger.

Why this matters for a receiver

A review can only harvest what can be said. Relational tacit knowledge can be said if someone asks the right question; somatic and collective tacit knowledge cannot, and must be passed on by working together. A receivership review that ignores this will produce tidy lessons about the explicit layer and leave the most valuable knowledge where it was.

Key terms
Subsidiary and focal awareness
Polanyi’s distinction between what we rely on (the clues) and what we attend to (the whole).
Proximal and distal
The clues and the whole they reveal; tacit knowing attends from the first to the second.
Indwelling
Polanyi’s term for how a skilled person lives in tools and clues as in his own body.
Knowing how / knowing that
Ryle’s distinction between practical ability and propositional knowledge.
Relational, somatic, collective
Collins’s three kinds of tacit knowledge, increasingly hard to make explicit.

Nonaka and Takeuchi: the SECI spiral, ba, and the critics

The best-known framework for moving knowledge between tacit and explicit forms is Ikujiro Nonaka’s, developed from 1990 and set out with Hirotaka Takeuchi in The Knowledge-Creating Company (1995). It names four modes of conversion. Socialisation (tacit to tacit) passes knowledge through shared experience: observation, imitation, apprenticeship, working alongside. Externalisation (tacit to explicit) articulates it, typically through metaphors, analogies, concepts, hypotheses or models. Combination (explicit to explicit) merges and reorganises what is already written down. Internalisation (explicit to tacit) absorbs it back into practice by learning through doing and reflection. Repeated, the four form a spiral that widens from the individual to the group and the organisation. Nonaka distinguished a technical side of tacit knowledge (know-how) from a cognitive side (the mental models, beliefs and perceptions people take for granted).

In 1998 Nonaka and Noboru Konno added ba, a Japanese word roughly meaning “place”: a shared context, physical, virtual or mental, in which knowledge is created. Later work with Ryoko Toyama paired each mode with a kind of ba: originating ba for socialisation (face to face), dialoguing ba for externalisation (peer conversation), systemising ba for combination (shared documents and networks) and exercising ba for internalisation (practice on the job). The 1995 book also named five enabling conditions: intention, autonomy, fluctuation and creative chaos, redundancy (overlapping information), and requisite variety.

Practitioner accounts stress two difficulties, both visible at Ferrier House. Externalisation is the hardest conversion and the one most knowledge-management efforts skip, because tacit knowledge was never consciously articulated in the first place. And restructuring, role changes and departures quietly remove tacit knowledge nobody captured: the replaced agent took the deposit history with him. The usual remedies are conversations with the people who hold the knowledge, shadowing, and structured debriefs, which is to say, reviews.

The critics, position by position

SECI is the most cited model in knowledge management and one of the most contested. Five lines of criticism matter for a receiver, and Nonaka has answered some of them.

Tsoukas: tacit knowledge is displayed, not converted. Haridimos Tsoukas’s “Do we really understand tacit knowledge?” (2003) goes back to Polanyi. For Polanyi all knowing is personal: maps, rules and formulas cannot apply themselves, and a skilled person must judge how they fit. Knowing has a from–to structure. We rely on subsidiary particulars (the feel of the hammer in the palm) to attend to a focal target (the nail), and the two kinds of awareness exclude each other: shift attention to the palm and the hammering becomes clumsy. The integration is irreversible, unlike a deduction. Tsoukas then turns to Nonaka and Takeuchi’s best-known case, the home bakery machine, in which a software developer apprenticed herself to a master baker and her “twisting stretch” was turned into machine features. On his reading Nonaka and Takeuchi treat tacit knowledge as knowledge not yet articulated, reducible in principle to if–then rules, which conflates it with technique and relies on a conduit picture in which ideas are objects to be extracted and sent. The baker’s skill was more than the technique, and her knowledge is present in the bread she kneads, not in her words about it. His conclusion is that tacit knowledge cannot be captured, translated or converted, only displayed in what we do. Tacit and explicit knowledge are two sides of one coin, not ends of a continuum.

Tsoukas does not conclude that nothing can be said. Practitioners can talk about skilled performance by drawing each other’s attention to things (“look at this”, “compare this with that”), and, after Wittgenstein, by reminding themselves of what they already know but cannot account for. Familiar features escape notice because they are always before us; a reminder brings them forward. New knowledge comes when practice is punctuated in new ways through interaction. Managers, he writes, should seek new ways of talking, fresh forms of interacting, and novel ways of distinguishing and connecting.

Gourlay: the evidence and the concepts do not hold. Stephen Gourlay’s critique in the Journal of Management Studies (2006) takes the four modes one at a time. The bread-machine story is ambiguous about whether taste or kneading was the problem. Claims about socialisation with customers report managers’ beliefs rather than demonstrated transfer. The externalisation cases assume the ideas were already held tacitly, and the role given to metaphor is untested, since everyday speech is full of metaphor anyway. Combination’s examples are thin and look more like transfer than creation (and the business-school case method he cites was designed to pass on tacit knowledge). The internalisation claims run against research on reading. Conceptually, he argues, Polanyi’s knowing, a process, is turned into knowledge, an object; socialisation and combination are transfers, not conversions; and the spiral’s starting point is arbitrary. His sharpest point concerns Nonaka’s definition of knowledge as justified belief. In practice the justification is managers evaluating ideas against criteria they set, so “knowledge” becomes what management sanctions, and the matrix models managerial decision-making rather than knowledge creation. His alternative separates knowing-how, which grows from everyday practice and learning by doing, from knowing-that, which comes from reflective inquiry (following Dewey). Knowledge is managed only indirectly, by attending to behaviour, and informed outsiders help practitioners see assumptions they cannot see themselves.

Stacey: knowledge is relating, not a stock. Ralph Stacey’s complexity critique (2001) names Nonaka and Takeuchi as representative of the mainstream rather than dissecting them, and attacks its foundations. The mainstream assumes a sender–receiver picture in which knowledge passes between people, and a stock picture in which it is stored in heads and then captured in systems. Stacey holds that knowledge as such is not stored anywhere: artefacts become knowledge only as people use them in interaction. The mainstream treats individual and collective as two levels; for Stacey they are the same process seen at different grains. He finds it meaningless to ask how tacit knowledge is transformed into explicit, because conscious and unconscious themes are aspects of one process, and translation cannot explain how anything new arises. Novelty comes from spontaneous variation in local interaction. Knowledge is the act of conversing; knowledge assets lie in patterns of relationship and are destroyed when those patterns are. Knowledge can be nurtured, but managing it in the conventional sense is impossible. This is the theoretical root of the Working live section (section 11).

Glisby and Holden: a map, not a model. Martin Glisby and Nigel Holden (2003) argue that SECI is culturally embedded in the Japanese firms it came from: long tenure, dense socialisation, shared expectations of consultation. They suggest reading it as a map rather than a model, or as a mirror in which an organisation can see its own knowledge habits. A receivership team assembled for nine months, from three firms with different incentives, is close to the opposite of the setting SECI describes.

Nonaka’s reply. In 2009 Nonaka and Georg von Krogh restated the theory’s premises: that tacit and explicit knowledge can be distinguished along a continuum, and that conversion explains their interaction. Answering Tsoukas, they accepted that the theory should not reduce all tacit knowledge to what could potentially be articulated: at one end of the continuum lies embodied knowledge that cannot be represented. The disagreement narrows but does not close. For Nonaka something is still converted; for Tsoukas and Stacey nothing is, and what changes is how people talk and relate.

What survives for a receiver

Read with all five, SECI remains a useful map of where knowledge moves in an appointment, provided “externalise” is read as Tsoukas reads it: finding new ways to talk about a practice, usually after it has broken down. Gourlay’s point about justification is a warning about lessons-learned systems: if the lender’s panel decides which lessons count, the repository records what the lender sanctions. Stacey’s point is the case for the xAAR as a conversation rather than an extraction. And Glisby and Holden explain why socialisation is weakest exactly where receivership needs it, among people who have just met. The instrument after the SECI spiral sets the five positions side by side.

What a receiver can take from SECI

Read with its critics, SECI is still a useful map of where knowledge moves, as long as “conversion” is read as “finding a way to talk about it”. For the I/we split it is precise. Socialisation and internalisation happen in a person and between people at work: that is the I ledger’s territory. Combination happens in documents and repositories: that is where the we ledger and the lender’s files live. Externalisation is the hinge, and the xAAR is an externalisation ba: a dialoguing space where the receiver’s, the lender’s and the agent’s tacit knowing gets words. The practitioners’ second warning connects to Larsen’s (section 11): people hold back knowledge when sharing it costs them leverage. In receivership terms, an agent who fears losing the instruction will not externalise what he knows about the stair cores.

Cards · Tacit knowledge
05 · Snowden’s knowledge mapping

ASHEN and the seven principles: what knowledge a decision actually used

In brief

Dave Snowden’s ASHEN, devised during his years at IBM and published in 2004, comes at tacit knowledge from the opposite direction to SECI. It does not ask people what they know, which Snowden calls a meaningless question in a meaningless context. It asks what knowledge they used in a particular decision, and breaks the answer into five kinds: Artefacts, Skills, Heuristics, Experience and Natural talent. The pieces are then clustered into “knowledge objects” and ranked by how vulnerable they are to loss. With it come Snowden’s seven principles for managing knowledge. For a receiver, and for the lender who instructs him, ASHEN asks a sharp retention question: when this receiver, this agent or this relationship manager leaves, what goes with them?

The five elements

Artefacts are explicit, codified knowledge and its containers: documents, databases, software. Skills are competences that can be taught, trained and measured by the speed and quality of output, such as plastering or public speaking. Heuristics (with habits and rituals) are the rules of thumb people use when full information is unavailable. Experience is knowledge gained from direct involvement; it is often the hardest tacit asset to capture, partly because it can be collective and hard to replicate. Natural talent is innate aptitude. Each kind needs different management. Artefacts need de-duplicating and getting to the people who need them. Skills need cataloguing and long lead times, and a guard against the belief that writing something down means others have learned it, which Snowden calls the codification heresy. Heuristics can be codified cheaply and their false assumptions removed. Experience is passed on through storytelling or war gaming, and dependence on a key experience is a vulnerability. Talent needs identifying, nurturing and protecting.

The general rule follows directly: the more a capability depends on artefacts and skills, the less one need worry about retention; the more it depends on experience and natural talent, the more concern is warranted. ASHEN also reframes dependency. Instead of “only Linda can do X”, the question becomes which combination of artefacts, skills, heuristics, experience and talent X requires, a shift from key-person dependency to knowledge dependency.

The method

ASHEN starts from knowledge disclosure points: accounts of events that give a meaningful context for eliciting knowledge, such as decisions, judgements, problem resolutions and learning events, often generated beforehand by decision mapping, future backwards or anecdote circles. In the room, three walls are papered and hexagonal cards in five colours wait on tables. Elicitation: for each cluster of disclosure points the facilitator asks about each element in turn (“what artefacts did you use?”), and asks each question several times with a different emphasis: what was used, what others use, what should be used, what may be needed, and what was once present but is no longer needed. Clustering: the answers are detached from their decisions and grouped into knowledge objects, the smallest grain that can still be managed as a whole, then broken up and regrouped to unsettle entrenched thinking. Action: knowledge objects are linked to core processes, ranked by vulnerability to loss, and turned into specific actions posted on a separate wall. Throughout, comment and judgement are avoided.

Two companion methods frame it, and a third supplies the stories. Each is set out in full below, because each is a practice in its own right, with its own strengths, weaknesses and critics.

Future Backwards in full

Future Backwards is described on the Cynefin wiki as a planning-support and “side-casting” method that exposes the range of perspectives a group holds on an issue at one moment. It was developed as an alternative to scenario planning, and is also used for lessons learned, historical analysis, context setting, finding turning points and generating anecdotes. It takes from an hour to half a day.

The rules matter more than the materials. Several groups are preferred, and no group may see another’s work before finishing its own. Participants are warned that they will work through stages without knowing where they lead, and are given no examples; anyone who asks for one is told there will be none. The sequence runs as follows.

  1. The present. The group agrees, by consensus, roughly five to seven statements about the current state, one per hexagon, placed about two-thirds of the way across the wall. Too few and the group fixates on today’s issue; too many and it lists trivia. The facilitator watches for dominant and disengaged members.
  2. The past, told backwards. The group names the most recent significant event that shaped the present and places it to the left, then the one before that, and so on: a single track backwards, in chronological order. The wiki’s image is a rear-view mirror. Only the most recent event is visible, and once it is agreed the group “reverses the car” to it. The facilitator stops “this caused that” chains, because the aim is chronology, not causation. Longer tracks are generally better.
  3. Utopia and Dystopia. The group describes an “impossibly good” future (upper right) and an “impossibly bad” one (lower right). The wording is deliberate: impossibly good, not the scenario planner’s best possible. Heaven and Hell may replace the terms where they would give offence.
  4. Fictional paths, backwards. From each extreme the group traces a path back to an event in its real history, using invented events, with one accident (something completely unexpected) allowed. The main error is working forwards from the present, and the facilitator must watch for it. If the facilitator has to suggest an accident, it should come from a different field, and the group is then barred from using it.
  5. Indicators. Two signs that the group is on the path to Utopia and two that it is on the path to Dystopia.
  6. Comparison. Each group leaves a spokesperson with its chart while the others circulate, asking what is different, what is the same, and what is surprising or interesting. Spokespeople rotate so that they too see the other charts.

The supporting theory is brief. Telling a story backwards increases cognitive load, which disrupts the well-worn forward narrative. Imagining beyond best and worst stretches what people scan for. Comparing groups helps with conflict: groups at odds often find they see the system similarly and want similar end-states, and sometimes the reverse. Either way, the wiki says, the charts leave people more open and less wedded to a single scenario.

For a receiver the method’s value lies in comparison. Run separately with the receiver’s team, the lender’s recovery team and the residents’ committee, it shows that each party’s history is as long as its stake: the receiver’s begins on day one, the lender’s at the facility, the residents’ on the day they moved into a building called finished. The instrument below lets you build all three charts step by step and lay them on one time axis.

Decision mapping in full

Decision mapping aims to show the patterns of real-world decision making in an organisation, so that work as done can be set against the formal process map. It is best fed by mass narrative capture, though interviews and workshops will do, and the key, the wiki says, is to gather material “without analytical questions or any form of judgement”. All staff, or a representative sample, record decisions as they make them (in text, voice or pictures) for about a week, and ideally in the background for months. For each decision they record the information received and the information that got attention, the artefacts and resources used, the people and advice consulted, how the decision was communicated or enacted, and what would have made it better. Decisions are then clustered. For each cluster the team identifies the information used, the information that would have improved the decision, and how the decision travels. Matching information in to information out links the clusters into a network, because one decision’s output is another’s input. The resulting map is messy but coherent and typically bears little relation to the formal process map, which was often drawn years earlier by consultants. The gaps become specific change projects, and the clusters become ASHEN’s disclosure points. The consultant presents the dissonance; the decision makers draw their own conclusions. Capture should happen at the time, in rich form and “in the wild”. Manual clustering is slow, and the default position is that the method cannot yet be run virtually.

The dependency matrix in full

The dependency matrix (formerly the QQE matrix: Qual, Quant and Emergence) finds useful connections between knowledge objects and the things decision makers care about. It deals with “real-world problems, as opposed to idealistic future goals”. One axis lists what matters, built either by asking decision makers “what keeps you awake at night?”, consolidating the answers and inviting dissent, or by deriving archetypes from anecdotes and scoring as those archetypes would. Each item is scored for importance. The other axis lists the knowledge objects from ASHEN, each scored against a criterion such as vulnerability to loss. Before any calculation the group agrees what counts as a pattern worth acting on (for example, three or four medium-to-high values in a line) so that nobody can move the goalposts later. Participants then score every intersection on a RAG, high–medium–low or 1–3 scale; the facilitator must not help. Scores are combined, by multiplying numeric values or by an agreed rule for qualitative ones (the wiki concludes that “whatever everyone accepts as meaningful is meaningful”) and colour-coded. Any pattern that meets the agreed rule is valid, and no one may create or suppress one. Vertical bars (one important concern hit by several knowledge objects) are easy to sell and hard to implement; horizontal bars (one knowledge object touching several concerns lightly) are hard to sell and easy to implement. The chosen patterns become a portfolio of strategic knowledge projects, each then placed on the Cynefin framework to decide how to treat it. Small groups from the same department work best, because comparing their matrices exposes departmental perspectives.

Reading the Snowden family critically

Taken together, the four methods have a clear logic: Future Backwards and decision mapping produce disclosure points, ASHEN turns them into knowledge objects, and the dependency matrix turns those into projects. Their shared strengths are real. They anchor every question in specific decisions and events, they distrust codification, they use separate groups and pre-agreed rules to limit the facilitator’s and the senior person’s influence, and they end in action. Their shared weaknesses are as real. Almost all the evidence for them is practitioner case reports, and several wiki pages are stubs with empty sections. The scoring steps treat ordinal judgements as numbers that can be multiplied, which Cox’s critique of risk matrices warns against. And every step depends on a disciplined facilitator, one who gives no examples, makes no judgements and stops forward causal chains. Read through the critics elsewhere in this treatise, the methods come out better than SECI by Tsoukas’s standard, because they draw attention to practice rather than extracting it. They remain open to Stacey’s and Shaw’s objection that any designed workshop is a pattern of power. And they need Larsen’s reminder that the people whose knowledge is most vulnerable may have the best reasons not to volunteer it. The appraisal panels below take each method in turn.

A case close to home: lending

Among the cases on the Cynefin wiki is a large bank whose lending decisions worsened as inexperienced lenders either avoided risk or made poor loans. Phase one gathered stories from experienced lenders about difficult decisions and put the ASHEN questions to them. Phase two built a narrative reference guide, using archetype extraction, that exposed newer staff to the reasoning behind experienced lenders’ “gut feel”. The same move suits a recovery team: the difficult receivership decisions are the disclosure points, and the guide is built from stories rather than procedures.

Snowden’s seven principles

Snowden extended three earlier rules to seven in 2008, in a piece written for a report on knowledge management in the legal profession. In brief:

  1. Knowledge can only be volunteered; it cannot be conscripted. One can measure information transfer or compliance, never whether someone has fully passed on their experience.
  2. We only know what we know when we need to know it. Recall depends on context and cues; there is no “list all” function.
  3. In the context of real need few people will withhold their knowledge, unless there is no time or a history of distrust; asking people to codify in advance is usually refused, so linking people matters more than storing their artefacts.
  4. Everything is fragmented: people handle fine-grained fragments easily and structured documents with effort.
  5. Tolerated failure imprints learning better than success; every culture has ways of spreading failure stories without blame, and imposed best practice runs against them.
  6. The way we know things is not the way we report we know things: decisions come from heuristics and pattern matching, but afterwards people give a tidy, process-shaped account.
  7. We always know more than we can say, and we will always say more than we can write down, which Snowden calls the most important of the seven.

What the principles do to an after action review

Read against Graves’s xAAR, the principles are both support and warning. The second principle explains why the xAAR’s questions must be anchored in specific decisions (the disclosure points) rather than asking “what did we learn?” in the abstract. The sixth warns that the review’s first account of any decision will be the tidy one; the CDM interview and the left-hand column exist to get behind it. The seventh says the ledgers will always hold less than the room said, and the room less than its members knew. The first and fourth explain why lessons-learned repositories fill slowly: knowledge is volunteered in fragments, in context, in response to real need. The fifth is Graves’s “no blame” and Snook’s good people struggling to make sense, put as a principle of evolution.

Where Snowden sits among the critics, and the tensions in ASHEN

Snowden’s principles are closer to Tsoukas and Stacey than to Nonaka: knowledge is contextual, not stored; writing loses most of it; people cannot be made to share. Yet ASHEN’s stated purpose is to help people articulate tacit knowledge so that it can be codified, and its outputs are “knowledge objects” to be managed. Tsoukas would say the method works because it does what he recommends, drawing attention to practice through specific decisions, and that “object” then over-reifies what it found. Stacey would say knowledge assets lie in patterns of relating, which no wall of hexagons can hold. Larsen and Elias would add that “key-person dependency” is also a power relation: the person who is the key may not volunteer the knowledge that keeps them indispensable, which is Snowden’s own first principle. Shaw would notice the facilitator’s instruction to avoid judgement and ask, with Corrigan, who designed the walls. None of this disables ASHEN. It locates it: a well-designed invitation to talk about practice through decisions, whose outputs are useful postcards (Weick’s word), not the knowledge itself.

Why this matters for a receiver

A recovery team runs on knowledge that is mostly experience and talent: the receiver who has seen three part-built blocks, the relationship manager who reads a valuer’s hedges, the agent’s caretaker who knows which doors are wedged. ASHEN gives the lender a way to see that dependency before it walks out of the door, and the seven principles explain why a policy manual will not hold it. The practical moves are modest: anchor every review in specific decisions, ask what each decision used, rank what is fragile, and connect people at the moment of need rather than asking them to write everything down in advance.

Cards · ASHEN and the seven principles
06 · How expertise grows

From novice to expert: Dreyfus, Benner, Klein and the recognition-primed receiver

In brief

Hubert and Stuart Dreyfus described skill as moving from rule-following to intuitive, holistic recognition. Patricia Benner showed the same path in nursing. Gary Klein found that experienced fireground commanders rarely compared options: they recognised the situation as a type, saw a workable action, and tested it by mental simulation. Each account explains how tacit knowledge accumulates, and each warns where it fails. Klein also built the tool a receiver can use to recover it: the Critical Decision Method.

Five stages

The Dreyfus brothers’ model, first set out for the US Air Force and elaborated in Mind Over Machine (1986), proposes five stages: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient and expert. The novice follows context-free rules. The advanced beginner starts to recognise situational aspects from experience. The competent performer chooses a plan and feels responsible for the outcome. The proficient performer sees what is happening intuitively but still decides analytically. The expert both sees and decides intuitively. Stuart Dreyfus, citing Patricia Benner’s work with student nurses, stressed emotional involvement: unless the learner stays involved and accepts the joy of a job well done and the remorse of mistakes, he does not progress. Patricia Benner’s From Novice to Expert (1984) applied the model to nursing and found that nurses at different levels literally lived in different clinical worlds, noticing different things.

The model has critics. Gobet and Chassy argued that expertise integrates perception and conscious problem solving rather than abandoning analysis. Klein himself has proposed retiring the five-stage model because it can lead trainers to force-feed rules that experts never used. For receivers the useful point survives the criticism: the expert receiver sees a different building from the novice, and much of what he sees is tacit.

Recognition-primed decisions

Klein’s research for the Army Research Institute in the 1980s asked how experienced urban fireground commanders made decisions under extreme time pressure. They did not, for the most part, generate and compare options. They recognised the situation as typical of a kind, which gave them plausible goals, relevant cues, expectancies and an action. If the situation was unusual, they ran a mental simulation of the action to see whether it would work, and adjusted or discarded it. Klein called this the recognition-primed decision model. It is Schön’s knowing-in-action seen from the inside, and it carries the same risk: recognition fails when the situation is misidentified. Ferrier House was recognised in the first week as a finished residential block with management problems. It was not.

Getting it out: the Critical Decision Method

To study tacit decision-making Klein and his colleagues developed the Critical Decision Method (CDM), an interview built on retrospection in several passes. The expert first tells the story of a non-routine incident; the interviewer then builds a timeline; then deepens it with probes about cues, knowledge, goals, options, and what would have changed the decision; then asks “what if” questions about how a novice would have handled it. The outputs include inventories of critical cues and portrayals of how the situation assessment developed. It is designed precisely to draw out knowledge that experts take for granted. A receivership review can borrow it whole: the xAAR asks what happened; the CDM asks what the receiver noticed, and when.

Instrument 7 · A Critical Decision Method interview on the fire doorsWhat did the receiver notice, when, and what would a novice have missed?

Four passes, as in Klein’s method. Step through them; each adds to the timeline and the cue inventory on the right. At the end, compare the expert’s cues with those a novice receiver would have used, and see which cues are relational (could be written down) and which are somatic or collective (could only be shown).

Instrument 8 · The same building at five levels of skillWhat does a receiver see at each Dreyfus stage?

Move the slider from novice to expert. The panel shows what a receiver at that stage notices on the first walk-round at Ferrier House, how he decides, what he risks, and the reflective practice that moves him on.

Novice

Communities of practice

Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger’s Situated Learning (1991) described learning as a process of moving from peripheral to full participation in a community of practice, studying midwives, tailors, quartermasters, butchers and recovering alcoholics. Newcomers learn from old-timers by being allowed to take part in real tasks, at first peripherally. Receivership is learned this way. The junior who carries the clipboard on the walk-round, drafts the tenant letter and sits in on the lender call is in legitimate peripheral participation. It is the main route by which somatic and collective tacit knowledge moves, and it is why the reflective practice of senior receivers matters to the profession as well as to their clients.

Why this matters for a receiver

An expert receiver’s greatest asset is recognition, and his greatest risk is misrecognition. Reflection-on-action, done with something like the Critical Decision Method, is how he recovers the cues his recognition rests on, checks them, and passes some of them on.

Cards · Expertise
07 · Thinking as you go

Reflection-in-action and the action-present

In brief

Reflection-in-action is thinking about what one is doing while one is doing it, prompted by surprise. Schön does not mean it has to be instant. It is bounded by the “action-present”: the stretch of time in which action can still make a difference. For a receiver the action-present can be an hour (a tenant in the corridor) or six months (the decision whether to complete the building).

Much reflection-in-action, Schön says, hinges on surprise. When intuitive, spontaneous performance yields nothing but the expected, we tend not to think about it. When it produces something unexpected, pleasing or unwanted, we may respond by reflecting. We ask ourselves what we are noticing, what criteria we are using, how we are framing the problem, and we do this while still acting, so that the reflection reshapes what we do next.

The concept that makes this useful for receivers is the action-present. Schön defines it as the zone of time in which action can still make a difference to the situation. It may stretch over minutes, hours, days, or even weeks or months, depending on the pace of the practice. A trial lawyer reflects-in-action in seconds; the same lawyer in an antitrust case that runs for years may do so at leisure over months. The test is not speed but whether the thinking can still change the outcome.

At Ferrier House several action-presents run at once, at very different speeds. The fourth-floor tenant’s complaint about mould has an action-present of days: the hazard is to a child’s health and will not wait for a review. The missing fire-door closers have an action-present of hours once noticed. The deposit question has one of weeks. The decision to complete or not complete floors six and seven has one of months. A receiver who reflects-in-action well knows which clock each surprise is running on, and gives each the thinking it needs within the time that remains.

Drag the slider to move through the eleven months of the appointment and watch which windows are still open, which are closing and which have shut. Select a surprise for its reading.

Why this matters for a receiver

Most receivership errors are not errors of analysis but errors of timing: deliberating over something whose window has already closed, or rushing something that had months. The action-present gives the receiver a way of asking, for each surprise, how long he has to think.

Cards · Reflection in and on action
08 · Thinking on the firing line

Does stopping to think put the action at risk? Schön’s four objections and his replies

In brief

Schön took seriously the charge that reflection gets in the way of action. He set out four versions of it: there is no time; thinking about a skill wrecks it; reflection leads to an infinite regress; and reflection is simply “out of order” in the middle of doing. He answered each. His conclusion is that nothing in reflection leads necessarily to paralysis. Reflection does cost something, though: a temporary loss of spontaneity, which the receiver has to choose when and where to pay.

The objections are in the penultimate chapter of The Reflective Practitioner, and they are the ones any receiver would raise. The first is the firing line. Schön puts it bluntly: there is no time to reflect when we are on the firing line, and if we stop to think we may be dead. The second is the centipede, who was asked which leg he moved first and could no longer walk: surfacing the complexity of a skill can wreck its smooth flow. The third is regress: if I reflect on my action, why not on my reflection, and on that, without end? The fourth is Hannah Arendt’s, that reflection belongs to the life of the mind and is “out of order” in the life of action.

His replies are worth reading slowly, because each gives a receiver something to do. To the firing line he answers that the action-present varies enormously, and that even a tennis player gives himself a moment to plan the next shot, “so long as he gauges the time available for reflection correctly”. The skill is not speed but judging how much time there is. Where there is genuinely none, a virtual world (a model, a rehearsal, a simulation) slows the pace so that the thinking can be done before the moment arrives.

To the centipede he answers, via Seymour Papert, that the centipede could have said “I move forward in a wavy motion” and kept walking. Reflection need not dismantle a skill into its parts; it can describe it at a level that helps. A coach does this with a metaphor (“Lean into the slope!”) rather than a list of muscles. The receiver’s equivalent is a short phrase he can carry into the corridor: the building as told is not the building as found.

To the regress he answers that it comes from an unexamined split between thought and action. In practice there is no regress, because “it is the surprising result of action that triggers reflection, and it is the production of a satisfactory move that brings reflection temporarily to a close.” We reflect, he says, when we are stuck. When the move works, the reflection stops by itself.

To Arendt he answers with double vision: reflection-in-action does not require us to stop and think, but the capacity to keep alive, in the midst of action, a multiplicity of views. He then adds a sentence every receiver should keep: “As the risk of uncertainty increases, so does the temptation to treat the view as the reality.” The more dangerous the moment, the stronger the pull to collapse to one frame. That pull is the real risk, not the reflection.

The price of reflection

Schön is honest about the cost. Changing a grip makes one “lose spontaneity for a time before recapturing it at a higher level of quality”. Whether to pay that price, he says, depends on our ability to find a context in which we can practise at low risk, or on our judgement of the value of incurring a temporary loss of spontaneity. That is a risk decision, and it has a shape, drawn in the second instrument below.

Two meanings of risk

Schön’s risk is the cost of a temporary loss of skill. Patricia Shaw and her colleagues (section 11) mean something social: the risk of being misunderstood, of losing face, of exclusion. Henry Larsen calls it spontaneity in the face of power differentials. A receiver usually feels both at once. Changing his grip at Ferrier House risks a worse week; changing it in front of the lender’s credit committee also risks his standing with the people who instruct him.

Instrument 10 · Four objections, four repliesWhere in the loop does each objection bite, and what does Schön say back?

Why this matters for a receiver

Receivers often say there was no time to think. Usually there was some time, and the error was in judging how much. Schön’s replies give three practical moves: gauge the action-present before deciding not to reflect; describe the skill at the level of a metaphor rather than taking it apart; and rehearse a change of grip somewhere cheap (a model, a tabletop, a quiet appointment) before paying for it at Ferrier House.

Cards · Risk and pressure
09 · Composing in the moment

Improvisation: schema, repertoire and the next move

In brief

Schön’s clearest picture of reflection-in-action is a jazz band. The musicians share a schema (the metre, melody and harmony of the tune) and each has a repertoire of figures. Improvisation is varying and recombining the figures within the schema that bounds and gives coherence to the performance. Organisation scholars took this up in the 1990s. Their main finding for receivers is that improvisation is not the absence of a plan. It depends on a deep repertoire, a minimal structure everyone shares, and a team that listens.

Schön describes jazz musicians improvising together. They “feel” where the music is going and adjust their playing, drawing on a shared metric, melodic and harmonic schema and on a repertoire of musical figures. In his words, “improvisation consists in varying, combining, and recombining a set of figures within the schema which bounds and gives coherence to the performance.” They reflect, he says, not in words but through a feel for the music. The same is true of a baseball pitcher “finding the groove” and “learning to adjust once you’re out there”.

A receivership has a schema too. Its metre is the timetable of the appointment; its harmony is the receiver’s duties (good faith, and at sale the best price reasonably obtainable), the lender’s instruction and the law of the charge. Its figures are the moves in the receiver’s repertoire: a walk-round, a call to the lender before the number, a retender, a quiet test of the market. Good improvisation varies the figures while keeping the schema. Bad improvisation breaks the schema: a promise the receiver has no power to keep, or a deal that sacrifices the duty to get a quick result.

Degrees of improvisation

Karl Weick’s 1998 essay, which opened a special issue of Organization Science on jazz and organising, treats improvisation as a mindset rather than a technique. He borrows a definition from Paul Berliner’s study of jazz: improvisation reworks “precomposed material and designs in relation to unanticipated ideas” under the special conditions of performance. Weick insists that it comes in degrees. Drawing on the saxophonist Lee Konitz he describes a continuum from interpretation (playing the piece much as written) through embellishment and variation to improvisation proper, where the piece is substantially recomposed in performance. Most of a receiver’s work is interpretation and embellishment. The moments that decide an appointment are usually variation or improvisation.

Christine Moorman and Anne Miner gave the idea a measurable form. They define organisational improvisation as the degree to which the composition and execution of an action converge in time: the narrower the gap between planning a move and making it, the more improvised it is. They argue that two kinds of organisational memory shape whether improvising helps: procedural memory (skills, how to do things) and declarative memory (facts). Their study of new product teams found improvisation more common where memory was thinner and the environment more turbulent.

What lets a band improvise

Frank Barrett, a jazz pianist and organisation scholar, described seven characteristics that let jazz bands improvise coherently. They are provocative competence (deliberately interrupting habit); embracing errors as a source of learning; minimal structures that allow maximum flexibility; a distributed task of continual negotiation towards a groove; retrospective sensemaking, where the meaning of a phrase is settled by what follows it; “hanging out” in a community of practice; and taking turns soloing and supporting. Ken Kamoche and Miguel Pina e Cunha developed the idea of minimal structures: just enough shared rules for coordination, and no more.

Two cautions came quickly. Dusya Vera and Mary Crossan, studying teams trained in theatre improvisation, found that improvisation helped innovative performance only under conditions, among them the team’s expertise and the quality of its teamwork. Improvising without skill or trust is just guessing in public. And Mannucci, Orazi and de Valck found that individuals who are skilled improvisers do not necessarily improvise well as a collective. That is the I and we split again: a receiver’s improvising and the team’s improvising are different capacities, built differently.

Offers, blocks and making do

From the theatre comes Keith Johnstone’s vocabulary. In a scene, anything a player says or does is an offer; the partner can accept it and build, or block it. Good improvisers, Johnstone observed, seem telepathic because they accept all offers made. The phrase “yes, and” later became the slogan. A receiver cannot accept every proposal: some are outside his powers or against his duty. He can accept every offer as information, the reality the other person is putting into the scene, and build from it, even when he declines what they are asking for.

From anthropology comes bricolage, Lévi-Strauss’s term for making do with whatever is at hand. Ted Baker and Reed Nelson defined it as making do by applying combinations of the resources at hand to new problems and opportunities. Beth Bechky and Gerardo Okhuysen, studying a police SWAT team and film crews, found that surprises were handled by organisational bricolage: role shifting, reorganising routines and reassembling the work, made possible because members knew each other’s jobs. A receiver’s team that knows only its own job cannot improvise together.

Two clocks

Mary Crossan and colleagues argued that improvisation reconciles two kinds of time: clock time (the timetable, the reporting dates) and event time (the moments when something happens and the timetable no longer fits). A receiver lives in both. The weekly report runs on clock time; the doubled price arrives in event time. Improvising well means letting event time interrupt the clock without losing the clock altogether.

A challenge from the theatre

Friis and Larsen of Denmark’s Dacapo Theatre argue that most of this literature (Weick, Kanter, Vera and Crossan) treats improvisation as a skill inside the individual and as a tool managers can deploy within guarded boundaries. In their experience it is a relational activity: novelty emerges between people as each responds to the other, and nobody, the manager included, stands outside it. Section 11 takes the challenge seriously.

Instrument 12 · Degrees of improvisationHow far from the score is the receiver playing?

Month six: the contractor doubles his price for completing floors six and seven. The slider runs from interpretation to improvisation (Weick, after Konitz). The bars underneath show Moorman and Miner’s measure: the gap between composing the move (blue) and executing it (gold). As improvisation increases, the two bars converge until they overlap. The panel shows what the receiver does at each degree, what memory he relies on, and what can go wrong.

Interpretation
Instrument 13 · Play the changesCan you vary the figures without breaking the schema?

The appointment is a tune of six bars. Each bar has its “changes”: what the situation and the receiver’s duties require at that point (top line). For each bar choose a figure from the receiver’s repertoire. A straight figure plays the routine; a varied figure adapts the routine to what is actually happening; an off-form figure breaks the schema. The two meters score coherence (staying within the schema) and freshness (responding to this building rather than the last one). Aim for both.

Choose a bar to play.

Instrument 14 · Offers at the residents’ meetingBlock, “yes, but”, or “yes, and”?

Week three, the community room. Five offers come from the residents’ chair, the contractor’s site manager and the agent. For each, choose a response. A block refuses the reality offered. “Yes, but” appears to accept and then takes it back. “Yes, and” accepts the offer as information and builds on it, even where the receiver must decline the request itself. The scene line grows with each accepted offer and stops short at each block.

Why this matters for a receiver

Lenders sometimes hear “improvise” as “make it up”. The literature says the opposite: improvisation is disciplined by a schema, fed by a repertoire, and only as good as the team’s listening. A receiver who wants freedom to improvise should agree the schema with the lender at the start (the duties, the decision points, what will be reported as provisional) so that variation within it is expected rather than alarming.

10 · When sense collapses

Under pressure: Mann Gulch, dropping tools, and organising for the unexpected

In brief

Reflection-in-action is easiest to praise and hardest to do when the stakes are high and the clock is short. Karl Weick’s studies of two wildland fires show how sense and structure can collapse together, and what keeps them standing: improvisation, a role system carried in each person’s head, an attitude of wisdom, and respectful interaction. Later work on high-reliability organising, on how people solve problems under time pressure, and on briefings gives the receiver concrete practices for the hour when the building surprises him badly.

On 4 August 1949 a crew of smokejumpers parachuted onto a fire in Mann Gulch, Montana, expecting to have it out by the next morning. The fire crossed the gulch below them and raced uphill. Their foreman, Wagner Dodge, ordered them to drop their tools, then lit a fire in the grass ahead of him and lay down in its ashes. Nobody followed him. Thirteen men died. Dodge survived in his escape fire, and two others by reaching the ridge. Weick’s 1993 reanalysis of Norman Maclean’s account reads the disaster as the collapse of sensemaking and of role structure in a minimal organisation. When the fire stopped being the fire they expected, the crew lost the frame and, with it, the organisation that told them whom to follow.

Weick called this a cosmology episode: the sudden sense that the world is no longer orderly, and that one’s means of rebuilding order have gone too. His four sources of resilience against it are the most useful single list in this treatise for a receiver under pressure. Improvisation and bricolage: the escape fire was invented on the spot from what was at hand. Virtual role systems: if each person carries the whole team’s roles in his head, the team survives the loss of any member or of communication. The attitude of wisdom: holding one’s knowledge with confidence and doubt at once, so that a surprise is a reason to look again rather than a reason to cling. Respectful interaction: trust, honesty and self-respect, so that what one person sees can be acted on by another.

Drop your tools

In 1994 fourteen firefighters died on Storm King Mountain in Colorado, and again some were found still carrying heavy tools and packs that slowed them. Weick’s essay “Drop your tools” lists ten reasons people keep tools they should drop. Among them are not hearing the order, not seeing the justification, not trusting the person giving it, wanting to keep control, lacking the skill to drop, having no replacement activity, fearing failure, social pressure and, above all, identity: a firefighter without his tools is no longer a firefighter. A receiver’s heavy tools are not saws and shovels but frames and commitments: the standard first report, the valuation on the file, the lender’s exit date, the agent he inherited, and his sense of himself as a property man rather than a builder. Dropping them is reflection-in-action at its most expensive.

Weick also noted that almost nobody at Mann Gulch or South Canyon heard a briefing that said: here’s what I think we face; here’s what I think we should do; here’s why; here’s what we should keep our eye on; now, talk to me. That five-part briefing is the simplest way to make one person’s reflection-in-action available to a team in the action-present.

Four ways of solving a problem under pressure

Jenny Rudolph, Bradley Morrison and John Carroll studied anaesthesia residents handling a simulated crisis and built a model of action-oriented problem solving that links acting, interpreting cues and cultivating alternative diagnoses. Four patterns appeared. Some residents stalled, unable to settle on anything to act on. Some fixated, acting vigorously on an early diagnosis and explaining away the cues against it. Some vagabonded, jumping from diagnosis to diagnosis without acting far enough on any to test it. Some adapted, acting on a leading diagnosis in ways that generated the cues that could disconfirm it. Their surprising finding was that some commitment to a diagnosis, even some confirmation bias, is needed: adaptive problem solving holds a view firmly enough to act on it, and loosely enough to let the action correct it. That is Schön’s double vision measured in a simulator.

Gary Klein’s fireground commanders show the same structure from the expert’s side. They rarely compared options. They recognised the situation, generated one plausible course of action, and evaluated it by imagining it played out. If the mental simulation ran into trouble they adjusted or moved to the next option. Mental simulation is reflection-in-action compressed into seconds, and it is only as good as the repertoire it runs on.

Five principles of mindful organising

Weick and Kathleen Sutcliffe distilled the practice of high-reliability organisations (aircraft carriers, nuclear plants, fire crews) into five principles. Three are about anticipating trouble: preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify and sensitivity to operations. Two are about containing it once it starts: commitment to resilience and deference to expertise, letting decisions move to whoever knows most, whatever their rank. A receivership team can adopt all five, and the instruments below give each a practical form.

Hiding behind technique

The psychotherapist Daniel Stern, quoted by David Walker (section 11), observed that the easiest and fastest way to reduce anxiety in a charged moment is to hide behind standard technical moves. That is Weick’s refusal to drop tools seen from the inside. The tool is comforting precisely because it spares us the risk of responding to what is actually happening.

Instrument 15 · Day forty-seven: the stormCan you reflect in action when the action-present is measured in seconds?

A Friday evening in a gale. Four decisions arrive one after another, each with a clock. Choose before the clock runs out; if it does, the moment passes and the record shows a stall. Each choice is classified by Rudolph’s four patterns. At the end you see your profile and the receiver’s own after-action note. Then play it again without the clock, in Schön’s virtual world, and compare: that difference is what rehearsal buys.

Up: how many alternative explanations he keeps alive. Drag the sliders (or choose a moment from the storm) and the dot moves into one of four regions. Adaptive problem solving sits in the upper right, but not at the corner: some commitment is needed to act at all.
