Why this matters for a receiver

Most of an appointment runs on clock time and leaves room for reflection-on-action. A few hours do not. The receiver who has rehearsed those hours (a tabletop on the storm, a five-line briefing ready, a team that knows each other’s jobs, a list of tools he is willing to drop) has moved some of his reflection from the action-present into a virtual world, where it is cheap. That is what Schön meant by finding a context in which to practise at low risk.

Cards · Under pressure
11 · Shaw, Stacey and the Dacapo Theatre

Working live: risk, spontaneity and improvisation as something that happens between people

In brief

In 2006 Patricia Shaw and Ralph Stacey edited a short book from the Complexity and Management Centre at Hertfordshire, Experiencing Risk, Spontaneity and Improvisation in Organizational Change: Working live. Its six chapters, by Shaw, two members of Denmark’s Dacapo Theatre (Preben Friis and Henry Larsen), the NHS director David Walker and Stacey, make three claims that cut across most of the improvisation literature in the previous section. Improvisation is not a skill inside a gifted individual but what happens between people as they respond to each other. Risk is spontaneity in the face of power. And presence means letting yourself be altered by what happens, which is exactly what “best practice” is designed to prevent. For a receiver, and for the xAAR, each claim has teeth.

Working live

Shaw’s introduction starts from the difference between a live broadcast and a recording. Live, the control of scriptwriters and editors is in abeyance, and the unexpected can happen. Her point is that ordinary working life is always live in this sense. Despite our plans, rehearsals and scripts, she writes, what happens next is “never a done deal”, because we cannot fully predict or control even our own responses, let alone anyone else’s (p. 2). Our exchanges are never exact repetitions but iterations, and small differences can amplify into real novelty. Experience can be more or less lively: familiar repertoires give stability and identity, and can also become “deadly routine”.

Her opening story is of a regular, agenda-free morning meeting. Two members have rehearsed a proposal and launch it before the chatter has died down. Within two minutes the room senses something odd, and a colleague says: “I get the impression you have rehearsed this.” What follows is an hour of live negotiation about trust, manipulation, authority and what the meeting is for. Shaw’s diagnosis is precise. The two men were not wrong to prepare. They went wrong when they kept to an already outdated idea of what should happen next instead of responding to what was actually happening: they were “playing themselves in an anticipated situation rather than finding themselves in the emerging situation” (p. 10). They lost spontaneity, and the room felt it before anyone spoke. Spontaneity, she insists, does not mean impulsiveness, thoughtlessness or lack of intention. It is a quality of self-consciousness in the moment.

Shaw then reads the story against two writers this treatise has leaned on. Edgar Schein held that in social systems there is no such thing as spontaneous change: what looks unplanned is a miscalculation (p. 6). Karl Weick’s account of commitment describes how actions that are explicit, public and irrevocable become “committed acts in search of an explanation” (p. 8), and he offers a recipe for strong commitment: action, publicity, choice, high stakes and low tolerance of mistakes. Shaw notes how neatly this supports the modern apparatus of performance contracts, milestones and public promises, and how managers find solace in it. Her objection is not that commitment is unreal but that “managing” meaning-making from outside is a fantasy. It is one thing to advocate managing the process, she writes, and quite another to participate in it.

The receiver’s first report is a committed act

Weick’s commitment recipe is a good description of the week-three report at Ferrier House. It was explicit, public (the credit committee read it), chosen, high-stakes, and once read it could not be unread. The lender’s later anchoring on the early numbers is exactly what Weick predicts: a committed act gathering justifications. Shaw’s point is that the report did not have to be the last word. Had it been written and discussed as one move in a live conversation, labelled provisional, open to response, the commitment could have been to the conversation rather than to the figure.

Gesture and response

The theory underneath is George Herbert Mead’s. Meaning does not lie in a gesture (a word, a letter, a report) but in the gesture taken together with the response it calls out. Because responses begin even as the gesture is under way, the meaning of any social act keeps emerging during the act, and a response can give an earlier gesture a meaning its maker never intended. Mead’s “I–me” dialectic describes the same process inside a person: the “me” is one’s sense of how one’s group would see what one is doing; the “I” is the response to it, which is always capable of spontaneity. Friis and Larsen set this against the sender–receiver model that runs through most management writing, in which a message is formed in one mind, sent, and either received or distorted. On the sender–receiver model, a receiver whose letter is misread failed to write clearly. On Mead’s, the misreading is part of what the letter now means, and the next move must respond to it.

Improvisation is not a tool

Friis and Larsen describe a day with fourteen newly hired occupational health consultants. An actor rings as a canteen manager with a small question about chlorine in a dishwasher. The consultants’ instinct afterwards is to list what the person answering should have done. Dacapo no longer replays such scenes, because replaying implies there is a right way to handle the call. We live our lives forwards, they write, despite understanding them backwards (p. 22). Instead the actor rings again, and again, and the consultants find that their five-step method (gather information, analyse, plan, agree, implement) keeps collapsing as each conversation changes the situation. The turning point of the day comes when someone asks: what if we can never know beforehand what will happen in the next moment? If that is so, what is consulting?

From Keith Johnstone they take an exercise called the bench. Two people must leave a bench for the same reason without speaking. At first each offers an idea and the other blocks it. Later the rule changes: neither may decide the reason; it must emerge between them. Eventually a pair simply attend to each other, smile, begin flirting and leave, and the audience cannot say whose idea it was. The lesson they draw is that you cannot control what emerges, but you can stop it: what you can control is “not to prevent something from happening” (p. 31).

They then turn on the organisational literature. Weick, they argue, treats jazz improvisation as a matter of individual intuition and a retrospective, fixed memory, and so underplays spontaneity and the way the present changes the meaning of the past. Kanter’s “strategy as improvisational theater” still depends on exceptional individuals with unwavering vision. Vera and Crossan locate improvisation in the individual and leave managers to guard the boundaries within which it may occur. Friis and Larsen’s answer is that managers cannot stand outside the improvisation: they are in it, and they too have to work live.

Risk is spontaneity in the face of power

Larsen’s chapter gives the book its most useful definition. In a furniture company that had outsourced its cleaning without telling its front-line managers, Dacapo’s actor plays Rosa, a cleaner who asks the top manager why she may no longer wear the company logo. The youngest of the three owner-partners says from the audience, as if settling the matter, that of course the manager must give her an explanation. Larsen invites him on stage to give it. He is visibly reluctant and nervous, plays to the audience, and Larsen is close to stepping in, until the actor leans in and tells him there are just the two of them, then questions him until he actually answers. Something shifts, not only between him and Rosa but among the partners and the managers watching. Later that day the chief executive, unprompted, explains forthcoming negotiations to the managers. In their written summary at the end of the work, Dacapo said they sensed the question people were asking beginning to move from “What can I say to whom and what will the consequences be?” to “What are the consequences of saying nothing?” (p. 54).

Larsen draws on Norbert Elias: power is not a possession but a feature of every relationship, a balance of dependency that constrains and enables at once. Groups form “we” identities by including and excluding, sustained by gossip and by ideologies that make the current order feel natural. Against that background he defines risk as spontaneity in the face of power differentials (p. 52): not unreflective impulse, but finding oneself responding in an unforeseen way, with full awareness of who is watching and what one stands to lose. The risk is of exclusion and of losing one’s identity, which is why it is felt in the body before it is thought. Spontaneity itself cannot be planned, but invitations to spontaneity can be: a scene, a live interview, a question asked in front of the right people. Fiction helps, because people will risk their status inside a story when they would not outside it. And the change is not a rehearsal for later. It happens in the room.

Presence, and the best-practice trap

Friis’s chapter contains the story most uncomfortable for anyone who writes up lessons. Asked to run a two-week course on making theatre from improvisation, he realised he had no method, admitted it to the participants, and improvised: frightened, always a step behind, making sense of what he had asked people to do only after they had done it. The course was a triumph. He then wrote the method down as a nine-step manual and ran it again. The second year was much worse and the third worse still. His conclusion: in trying to stay in control, he lost it (p. 83). He explains the decline with John Shotter’s “ex post facto fact fallacy”: a situation open to many readings is described one way; that description is accepted as true; it permits further statements until a system is built; and the first reading now seems true because of its place in the system. Once inside such a system, it is very hard to recover the open, undecided thinking from which it came.

Friis defines spontaneity as an immediate reaction based on intuitive reflections (p. 88): immediate, because time matters; a reaction, because it is a response to someone; intuitive reflection, because it draws on a whole social history that is not fully present to consciousness when one acts. Good acting, he says, comes from rehearsing thoroughly and then, in performance, recreating the play spontaneously from the rehearsals. On presence he takes Johnstone’s instruction, “Be altered by what’s said” (p. 90). We recognise someone as present when their identity is visibly shifting in response to us, and as absent when they hold on to what they planned. Holding on to best practice is one way of staying unaltered. He also offers a hard image for the lone expert: the Western hero who rides in, sees at once what must be done, never explains, and is proved right. The Grindy Company’s HR director wanted that kind of intervention. Receivers are sometimes cast in the same role.

Leading in the moment, and living with anxiety

David Walker, a director in an NHS trust, tells of setting up an unconventional leadership programme he called Ariadne. His first steering group is ambushed by a question he dreads: what are the outcomes, and how will you measure them? He withdraws, stutters and loses the room, and at the second meeting takes appropriate control. His lesson: prepare, and then forget the preparation, so that something new can emerge (p. 105). From the psychotherapist Daniel Stern he takes the idea of “sloppiness” (intentional fuzziness, unpredictability, redundancy and improvisation) and Stern’s caution that sloppiness is creative only within a well-established framework (p. 102), which is Schön’s schema in another vocabulary. Stern also describes a “now moment”, when a relationship is suddenly at stake, and a “moment of meeting” that can resolve it. The danger in a now moment is the escape route Stern names: the easiest and fastest way to reduce anxiety is to hide behind standard technical moves (p. 119). Walker shows himself doing exactly that when a participant challenges a rule, and then finding the moment of meeting when he stops.

Walker reads the organisation’s anxiety about Ariadne three ways: through Isabel Menzies Lyth’s social defences against anxiety, through Stern’s intersubjective anxiety, and through Stacey’s view that anxiety is an inevitable companion of shifts in the themes that organise relating (p. 120). In each reading, anxiety is not a sign that something has gone wrong. Without it, nothing would be moving.

The theory: complex responsive processes

Stacey’s closing chapter sets out the theory of complex responsive processes of relating. It borrows from complex adaptive systems the insight that coherent global patterns emerge from local interaction without a global plan, then insists that human beings are not rule-following agents but conscious, self-conscious, emotional, spontaneous bodies who communicate (Mead), relate through power (Elias) and choose according to values and norms. Generalisations such as an instruction letter, a policy or a mission are what Mead called social objects and cult values. They exist only as people particularise and “functionalise” them in specific situations, and doing so always involves conflict and negotiation. Stacey is blunt about long-range plans: beyond short-term, repetitive work like budgeting, he calls them largely fantasies (p. 139) whose main function may be to defend against anxiety.

Who hosts the review? Chris Corrigan’s honest accounting

In September 2026 Chris Corrigan, a facilitator in the Art of Hosting community for nearly twenty-five years, wrote an open letter to that community, following an earlier letter to Dave Snowden. It is one of the clearest pieces of practitioner reflexivity in this field, and it applies directly to anyone who convenes a review. His argument is that a hosted dialogic container is a real intervention in a system, but it is not the system. Hosts shape what is possible through design, hosting choices and harvesting, and that power is often invisible, even when the methods appear to hand control to the participants. People drawn from a system are not the system, and a powerful experience is not system change.

He calls hosting an exercise of power: someone calls the meeting, frames its purpose, selects the methods and decides the harvest. To locate that power he offers a triangle of three sources of constraint: interactions (the distributed power of the group), structure (the contextual power of existing organisations, laws and resources) and design (the privileged power of the host’s choices). He presents it as a reflective tool, not a model of reality. Open Space, World Café and Circle create conditions; on their own they neither reveal collective intelligence, transform a system nor remove status. His central fear is the gathering where people loved the process and the work but nothing in their world changed, and he adds two quieter risks: a good gathering can delay action, and it can suggest that only skilled hosts can make engagement happen. In the discussion that followed he put it more briefly still: we participate in emergence; we do not host it. The Art of Hosting’s four-fold practice (being present, participating, hosting, co-creating) remains his reminder of what makes such conversations matter.

Where Corrigan fits in reflective practice

Corrigan’s letter is reflection-on-action by a practitioner about his own practice, made public to his community of practice: exactly the kind of “honest accounting” Schön asked of professionals and Brookfield’s critical reflection asks of teachers. It also sharpens three things in this treatise. First, the xAAR is a hosted container. Whoever convenes it, usually the lender, frames its purpose, chooses Graves’s questions and decides what goes in the repository; Gourlay’s point that “knowledge” becomes what management sanctions applies. Second, a review that the lender, receiver and agent all found valuable may still change nothing in the structure: the panel terms, the credit paper template, the reporting rules. That is “lessons identified, not learned” seen from the host’s side. Third, his triangle locates power the way Larsen and Elias do, and it shows where the I and the we ledgers sit: the I ledger is mostly interaction, the we ledger is where design meets structure. The instrument below places the Ferrier House review’s decisions in his triangle.

Instrument 19 · The hosting triangle for the Ferrier House reviewWhose power shaped each decision about the review?

Corrigan’s triangle: interactions (the group), structure (organisations, law, resources) and design (the host’s choices). Each numbered point is a decision about the joint xAAR, placed by where its power came from. Switch between the review as it was hosted (by the lender’s recovery team) and as it could be co-hosted, and watch the decisions move. Select a decision for who made it, what it shaped, and Corrigan’s question about it.

Select a decision.

What this does to the xAAR and the I/we split

The book strengthens the treatise’s central commitment and complicates it. Mead’s I–me dialectic is a precise account of why the receiver’s own learning is distinct: the I ledger records what the receiver’s “I” did with the “me” of his profession, and how that shifted. Elias shows why the we ledger can never be neutral: a lender, receiver and agent team is a figuration of power with its own we identity, and its shared commitments are negotiated, not agreed. Two practical consequences follow. First, an xAAR that is rehearsed (a polished narrative, agreed in advance between the lender and the receiver) will feel exactly like Shaw’s morning meeting, and will teach nothing. Second, the ledgers must not harden into a nine-step manual. Friis’s decline from the first year to the third is a warning about every lessons-learned database: record commitments and questions, not a method.

Where the book and the rest of the treatise disagree

Shaw and Stacey are suspicious of designed tools for managing meaning, and some of this treatise is exactly that: the xAAR, the five-part briefing, the HRO principles. The disagreement is real and worth keeping open. The reading offered here is that the tools are invitations to spontaneity in Larsen’s sense, partly planned occasions for live work, and fail when they are used as scripts. Readers who share Stacey’s view may prefer to treat every instrument in this treatise as a rehearsal space rather than a method.

Instrument 20 · Gesture and responseWhat did the receiver’s words mean, once the lender had responded?

Week three, a call between the receiver and the lender’s relationship manager. At each turn, choose the receiver’s gesture. The relationship manager responds, and the response changes what the earlier gesture meant: watch the meaning tag on the previous bubble rewrite itself. This is Mead’s claim that meaning lies in the gesture and response together, not in the words alone.

Instrument 21 · Risk as spontaneity in the face of powerHow risky does this move feel, and what invitation would make it possible?

Why this matters for a receiver

A receiver is paid to be the person who knows what to do, which makes him the hero of Friis’s Western and the natural author of the nine-step manual. The book’s challenge is to be present instead. That means preparing thoroughly and then responding to what the lender, the agent and the forty-two households actually say. It means treating his reports as gestures whose meaning will be settled by the response. And it means noticing when he is hiding behind a technical move because the room has become uncomfortable. The risk is real. It is the risk of being misunderstood, and it cannot be designed away.

Cards · Working live
12 · Chia and Tsoukas

Everything flows: change as becoming, and what a reflective receiver attends to

In brief

Robert Chia and Haridimos Tsoukas’s “Everything Flows and Nothing Abides” (Process Studies, 2003) turns the usual question upside down. Most writing on change asks how stable organisations come to change. Drawing on Heraclitus, Bergson, Whitehead, Deleuze and Prigogine, they ask how anything stays stable in a world that is always changing. Organisation, for them, is the exception: a continual human effort to arrest, simplify and stabilise a reality that is always on the move. For a receiver this has three practical consequences. The building was changing before he arrived and goes on changing whatever his plan says. The task is to notice the small, half-visible changes below the level of reports. And every report, ledger and lesson is a temporary closure that will start to slip as soon as it is written.

Two metaphysics of change

The paper opens with a contrast. The dominant Western habit of thought, which they call Parmenidean, puts order, stability, discreteness and identity first, and treats change as an exceptional event happening to stable things. Its tools are typologies, hierarchies, systems and structures. The alternative, process metaphysics, treats movement and becoming as primary and sees entities, end states and outcomes as passing products of underlying processes. Whitehead noted that this view is closer to some Indian and Chinese thought than to European: one side makes process ultimate, the other makes fact ultimate. On the process view, what we experience as a solid organisational reality is an aggregate of routines that arrest, locate, regularise and stabilise portions of a changing world. Organisation and change are not complementary terms but opposing tendencies, and their tension is what drives organisations to evolve.

They then test the leading theories of organisational change against this standard. Kanter, Stein and Jick quote Heraclitus approvingly and criticise Lewin’s unfreeze–change–refreeze as quaintly linear, yet their own “Big Three” model still types and lists changes, dealing with their sources and effects rather than change itself; they even say that anything unique is not worth much organisational attention, when change is precisely what is unique. Pettigrew’s content, context and process become thing-like. Van de Ven holds that change without an object is meaningless; Bergson’s reply is that “movement does not imply a mobile”. Ford and Ford’s trialectics, in which things are temporary resting points of movement, come closest. Chia and Tsoukas also enlist Weick: if theorists bolt improvisation onto concepts built to explain order, the result is a caricature of improvisation. To take improvisation seriously one has to revise one’s metaphysics.

Three axioms

Heterogeneous becoming. After Whitehead, how something becomes is what it is: its being is constituted by its becoming. And becoming is not one thing. Bergson distinguished qualitative movements (yellow to green), evolutionary movements (flower to fruit) and extensive movements (eating, fighting), and warned that language collapses them into a colourless “becoming in general”. At Ferrier House the mould in flat 4.06, the drift of the agent’s habits, the contractor’s pricing and the residents’ trust were different kinds of movement, and a report that called them all “issues” lost exactly that difference.

The logic of otherness. Nothing is simply present and self-identical. An identity is established against an other that is suppressed in the background: Robert Cooper’s example is the screw and the nut, each the completion of what the other lacks. For this treatise the point is precise. “The building as told” and “the building as found” define each other, and so do the I and the we. The two ledgers are kept separate because they are different commitments, but each only makes sense against the other.

Immanence. The past is carried in the present, not left behind it. Their image is Jasper Johns’s painting 0 through 9, in which the ten numerals are drawn on top of each other so that every earlier figure shows through the last. Each situation carries the traces of its genealogy, “the accidents, the minute deviations” of how it came to be. The receiver’s month-eleven building contains its month-one building; the xAAR’s question “what caused the difference?” is a search for traces.

The rhizome

From Deleuze they take the rhizome, the underground stem that, unlike a root-tree branching from one point by binary steps, connects any point to any other. Rhizomic change is subtle, agglomerative, often subterranean and heterogeneous. It “spreads like a patch of oil”, by variations, restless expansion, opportunistic conquests, sudden captures and offshoots, and it resists being traced back to a single origin. With Prigogine they add that in a world far from equilibrium the future is a matter of probabilities, not single trajectories; outcomes are coupled by something like resonance rather than simple causes; and surprise is built into the core of change. With Casti: we are surprised because our models are unfaithful to an evolving world. Chance leans towards otherness, necessity towards immanence.

Organisation as world-making

On this view organisation is not a thing but the repetitive activity of ordering and patterning, an intervention into flux to extract coherence. It is inherently simplifying, which is why they call “complex organisation” an oxymoron. Its work is to stabilise the real enough for people to act on purpose. Zygmunt Bauman’s image fits: a garden is sustained only by a gardener’s continual effort, and weeds are always there to show how fragile the imposed order is. A receivership is a garden planted in a wilderness. The receiver’s controls, reports and protocols are the gardener’s work, and they are necessary, but they do not make the wilderness go away.

Rethinking action: the upper and lower levels

The most practical part of the paper borrows Isaiah Berlin’s “sense of reality”. Social life has an upper level of public, inspectable facts and a lower level, a “dark mass” of shifting, half-known relationships that resist tidy classification. Practitioners who confine their attention to the upper level and its formulae miss the lower, and their reforms fail. What marks out the gifted practitioner is a superior sense of the contours of these unknown and half-known factors. For a receiver the upper level is the rent roll, the report, the valuation and the credit paper; the lower level is the tenant who stopped complaining, the subcontractor’s silence, the agent’s habits and the water that has been finding its way in since before the appointment.

Organisational action, they argue, needs closure of meaning, categories stable enough to use. But closure is always temporary, for two reasons. First, action meets the outside world. Julian Orr’s photocopier technicians found that repair manuals were of limited use, because machines break down in contexts no manual anticipates, and technicians must also keep customers’ trust and their reputation among peers. Action is a communication whose meaning lies in its effect on the minds that receive it (Vickers), so it is always partly indeterminate. Dewey adds that potentialities are known only after interactions have happened. Second, people reflect. Following Maturana, every description we make becomes the basis for new interactions and so new descriptions. Their sentence is worth quoting: “Potentially endless reflexivity creates the conditions for potentially endless novelty.”

So actors are webs of beliefs and habits that keep re-weaving themselves to accommodate new experiences (Rorty), and memory itself is a reiterated act of interpretation (Berger). Change is that re-weaving: minimal, as in single-loop learning or Weick’s embellishment, or maximal, as in a new metaphorical redescription. Improvisation, on this account, is not a special talent but the effort to accommodate new experiences, as present in a photocopier technician, a blacksmith, a planner or a ship’s navigator as in a jazz musician. Planned change is only a special case, in which new meanings sanctioned by senior management try to displace old ones. What deserves attention is microscopic change: creep, slippage, drift and spread.

What a practitioner does, on this view

Chia and Tsoukas end with advice. Discard the heroic view of change. The organisation is changing anyway, and the practitioner had better find out how and why. Deliberate intervention means creating a communicative context in which some of the changes already happening at the lower level are amplified and others are not. The change agent is perennially re-interpreting other people’s interpretations, producing a closure that is always temporary and incomplete. Their research questions are a reflective practitioner’s checklist: how do novelties get noticed, or not; what happens to them once noticed; are they legitimated, marginalised or amplified; do they become institutionalised, and with what effects?

Where a receiver must part company

Chia and Tsoukas go further than a receiver can follow. They suggest that relaxing entrenched controls is itself enough to let change happen of its own accord, a “hands-off” stance. A receiver has duties that do not relax: forty-two households, fire doors, the duty on price at sale. Weick and Sutcliffe’s high-reliability organisations and Shaw and Stacey’s relational account each offer a different correction. HROs keep some structures rigid precisely so that others can flex. Stacey would say change happens in interaction with or without intervention, and that relaxing control is itself an intervention with power effects. The useful reading for a receiver is selective: keep the controls that carry a duty, relax the ones that only make the building look more knowable than it is.

How this connects to the rest of the treatise

The paper gives a metaphysical ground to much of what came before. Schön’s back-talk is the lower level speaking. Reflection-in-action is the re-weaving of a web of beliefs while acting. The xAAR is a moment of temporary closure, and its repository a garden that will need tending. Graves’s trails of provenance and derivation are Chia and Tsoukas’s immanent traces. Tsoukas’s critique of SECI (section 04) and Stacey’s complex responsive processes (section 11) belong to the same family of process thought,.

Why this matters for a receiver

The receiver is appointed to a building that is already in motion and will stay in motion. His reports are temporary closures and his plan is one line among many. The reflective discipline Chia and Tsoukas ask for is a sense of reality: attention to the lower level, to the small slippages that have not yet become facts, and to which of them deserve to be amplified into the upper level of reports, decisions and ledgers. It is also humility about the review itself. The xAAR closes the appointment’s meaning for now; the building, the relationship and the receiver will go on changing.

Cards · Everything flows
13 · Weick’s handoff

Sensemaking, experience and understanding: what Weick handed on

In brief

In 2020, half a century after The Social Psychology of Organizing, Karl Weick wrote a short essay for the Journal of Management Studies, “Sensemaking, Organizing, and Surpassing: A Handoff”. It is a summary and a bequest. It sets out sensemaking as a movement from flux to hunches to words to actions and back to flux, and then examines four ways experience and understanding relate: self-validating prophecy, partiality towards similarity, ambivalence between belief and doubt, and understanding as an ongoing accomplishment. Each is a hazard or a resource for reflective practice, and each has a direct receivership form.

From airy nothing to a local habitation

Weick opens with Theseus in A Midsummer Night’s Dream: the poet’s pen gives to airy nothing “a local habitation and a name”. That is sensemaking. Flux is imagined into hunches about forms, which are then named and pinned to a place that can be shared. William James describes the same thing: pure experience fills itself with emphases, and the salient parts become fixed, so that experience flows as if shot through with nouns and verbs. Weick’s definitions follow. In 1969, organising was the resolving of equivocality in an enacted environment by interlocked behaviours. Since 2005 sensemaking has been described as the ongoing retrospective development of plausible images that rationalise what people are doing. The common elements are retrospect, plausibility, images, reasons, interaction and construction: activity enacts an order that is then read back as a justification.

Weick turns this into a workable sequence: flux → hunches → words → actions → back to flux, the 1969 cycle of enactment, selection and retention in plainer terms. Moving from flux to hunches simplifies enough to give workable certainty. Moving from hunches to words matters because, with Rorty, there is no access to truth that does not pass through language. Moving from words to actions produces meanings of varying depth, and here Weick cites Dewey’s imperative: act so as to increase the meaning of present experience, studying the needs and possibilities of the unique local situation, until doing so becomes a habit. Whatever the meaning, the action alters the flux and changes the person who acts.

Lived forwards, understood backwards

Kierkegaard supplies the central disjunction: life must be understood backwards but lived forwards, and there is no moment when time stops so that one can take up a position to look back. Weick links this to Jörgen Sandberg and Haridimos Tsoukas’s phenomenological account of sensemaking (2020). In a practice, sensemaking is first immanent: the forward, absorbed coping of someone getting on with the work. When the work is interrupted it becomes involved-deliberate, and if resuming is still a problem it becomes detached-deliberate, more thematic and abstract. The mapping onto Schön is close: knowing-in-action is immanent, reflection-in-action is involved-deliberate, and reflection-on-action is detached-deliberate. Weick’s warning is that because forward experience is fleeting and hard to see, it is tempting to treat deliberate backward understanding as the only place sensemaking happens. To give in to that temptation is to lose the interplay between the two, which is exactly where reflective practice lives.

Four relations between experience and understanding

Self-validating prophecy. Bateson: beliefs about what sort of world it is determine how one sees it and acts in it, and those ways of acting determine one’s beliefs about it. James: the knower is a co-efficient of the truth he registers. Weick’s example is Dominic Wilkinson’s study of intensive care, where predicting a poor outcome can raise its probability, and where Wilkinson insists that doctors be honest with themselves and with families about uncertainty and the limits of knowledge. A receiver’s first report is such a prophecy. Call the building a nine-month unit sale and every decision starts to make it one, and the evidence that it is not gets read as noise.

Partiality towards similarity. Organisations turn equivocal information into the degree of clarity they are accustomed to; James says we want a minimum of jolt and a maximum of continuity. The result is normalisation, which Diane Vaughan traced in the Challenger disaster, where anomalies became accepted and routine. High-reliability organisations are designed against it. Weick adds two further traps: the observer keeps changing, so “similar to last time” compares with a person who no longer exists (Dewey), and origins are elusive, because, as Mary Parker Follett put it, we never catch the stimulus stimulating. At Ferrier House the damp complaints, the swinging fire doors and the hairline cracks were each, at first, “what you always get in a block like this”.

Ambivalence between belief and doubt. Weick has held since 1969 that adaptability comes from believing and doubting past experience at the same time, using it to act but questioning it when interpreting what the action produced. Donald Campbell’s insight is that where two opposing tendencies both matter for survival, alternating between them works better than averaging them. Wildland firefighters build this into a protocol, LCES: Lookouts and Communication enact belief in the fire they know; Escape routes (at least two) and Safety zones enact doubt about a fire that may turn into one they do not know. Ambivalence creates resilience. Wisdom, in Meacham’s account, is the same balance: accumulating knowledge while remaining suspicious of it. The instrument below builds a receiver’s LCES.

Understanding as ongoing accomplishment. Finally, experience and understanding can be treated as one continuing activity in which people create and sustain images of a wider reality, partly to rationalise what they are doing. Weick’s example is Scott Snook’s study of the 1994 friendly-fire shootdown of two US helicopters over northern Iraq by two F-15s, in which twenty-six people died. Reframing the question from decision to meaning, Snook found he could have made the same mistake, and argued that such tragedies should first be framed as good people struggling to make sense, rather than bad ones making poor decisions. Robert Chia calls decisions ontological incisions into the flux, temporarily stabilising a changing world.

Three extensions that matter for reviews

Weick comments on three papers published with his essay. With Glynn and Watkiss, sensemaking becomes not something that happens in organisations but what organising is, and coupling matters: in loosely coupled systems maps can be held apart from action, so improvisation and workarounds flourish; in tightly coupled ones the map becomes the territory, and the tighter the coupling, the higher the chance of surprise. With Mikkelsen, Gray and Petersen, sensemaking has an unconscious side: under threat, anxiety drives rationalisation, projection and fantasy, and two parties (their case is a hospital and community mental health services) come to hold stereotypes of each other’s incompetence. Weick now notes that his own Mann Gulch paper underplayed contested meaning, citing Hellman’s refusal of Dodge’s escape fire. With Meziani and Cabantous, intuition is embodied and enacted, and Weick quotes Ron Westrum: a system’s willingness to become aware of problems is linked to its ability to act on them.

The handoff

Weick ends with a dream: on stage at a birthday celebration with a table of unopened magic tricks, he performs the two he knows, then tips the rest into the audience and leaves before anyone can ask “what was that all about?”. That question is sensemaking in five words: “that” is the flux, “what” is the sense. He calls the essay a conceptual postcard. In a gallery, hold a postcard reproduction next to the painting and you see what the reproduction misses. Hold a concept next to everyday life and you see what the concept fails to register. For this treatise the postcard image is the right one for every instrument, card and ledger: imperfect copies whose value is that they help a receiver see the building more clearly.

Why this matters for a receiver

What am I treating as normal because it resembles the last building? Am I believing and doubting at once: do I have lookouts and two escape routes? Cards · Sensemaking
14 · Looking back

Reflection-on-action: looking back after the fact

In brief

Reflection-on-action is thinking back over what was done, once the action-present has passed, to understand it and to prepare for future cases. It is the kind of reflection receivers are most likely to do already, in file notes and closing reports. It is also the kind most easily done badly: as justification rather than inquiry, and alone rather than with others.

Schön treats reflection-on-action briefly, almost as the familiar case against which reflection-in-action stands out. Practitioners, he says, reflect on their knowing-in-practice in relatively tranquil moments: they think back on a project, a case or a period of work, explore the understandings they brought to it, and do so either in idle speculation or in a deliberate effort to prepare for future cases. The subsequent literature has made far more of it than he did. Most of the structured reflective models (Kolb, Gibbs, Driscoll, Rolfe and the rest) and every form of the after action review are tools for reflection-on-action.

For a receiver it already has an institutional form: the file note, the periodic report to the lender, the closing report. These are valuable, but they are written for an audience and tend to explain rather than examine. A closing report says what was done and why it was reasonable. Reflection-on-action asks a harder question: what did I believe at the start that turned out to be wrong, and what does that tell me about how I see buildings like this?

At Ferrier House the receiver’s first reflection-on-action comes at the end of week two, on the train home, and it is uncomfortable. He realises that he spent the first three days on the rent roll and the deposits, the things his repertoire told him mattered, and only reached the fire doors on day four, because the fire strategy for a finished building is normally the agent’s problem. Nothing went wrong. It could have. He writes it down, not for the file, but in the notebook he keeps for himself.

Alone and together

Reflection-on-action can be private or shared. Private reflection examines one’s own judgement; shared reflection examines how a team’s judgements combined. Both are needed, and they produce different kinds of commitment. That distinction becomes central in sections 26 and 27.

Why this matters for a receiver

A receiver who reflects on action only in reports to his client learns what his client wants to hear. Private reflection, kept separately and honestly, is where his practice actually improves.

Cards · Looking back
15 · The prepositions

Reflection-for-action, and Eraut’s three prepositions

In brief

Later writers added a third form: reflection-for-action, thinking ahead in order to act well. The British educationalist Michael Eraut went further and argued that Schön’s prepositions were muddled. He proposed that “in” describes the context of reflection, “on” its focus, and “for” its purpose. On that reading most of what receivers call reflection is on and for action, and only some is genuinely in it.

Killion and Todnem (1991) introduced “reflection-for-action” to name the deliberate preparation that precedes a piece of work: rehearsing, anticipating and planning in the light of past experience. Its organisational forms include Gary Klein’s premortem and the before-action reviews and peer assists of the knowledge-management tradition (section 30).

Michael Eraut’s critique, published in 1995 under the title “Schön Shock”, is the most searching. He argued that most of Schön’s examples do not actually show reflection-in-action, that none come from crowded, fast-moving settings like a classroom, and that it is hard to tell reflection-in-action from reflection-on-action when the action is cool and deliberate rather than hot and rapid. He recommended reading the prepositions differently: “in” for the context, “on” for the focus and “for” for the purpose. On his reading all of Schön’s examples are reflection on action and for action, and only some are in action.

This is useful for receivers because it removes a false choice. The question is not which type of reflection a receiver is doing but three separate questions. Where is the reflection happening: inside the action, or after it? What is it about: the action, the situation, or the receiver’s own framing? What is it for: the next move, the next case, or the receiver’s development? A good AAR at the end of Ferrier House is reflection after the action, on the team’s action and framing, for the next appointment and the next relationship.

Why this matters for a receiver

The three prepositions give a receiver a simple test for any piece of reflection: where, about what, and for what. Reflection that cannot answer “for what” is usually rumination.

Cards · The prepositions
16 · The conversation

A reflective conversation with the situation: frames, moves and back-talk

In brief

Schön’s central picture of reflective practice comes from an architecture studio. The master, Quist, does not solve a design problem; he imposes a frame on it, makes moves within the frame, and listens to how the situation “talks back”. When the back-talk surprises him, he may reframe. A receiver does the same with a building: he frames it, acts, and listens to what it does in response.

In the third chapter Schön follows Quist reviewing the work of a student, Petra, who is stuck. Her school building will not fit its sloping site. Quist does not tell her the answer. He draws. He imposes a new geometry on the slope, a set of terraces, and then follows the consequences of that move through the drawing: where the classrooms go, what the slope does to the gallery, where a nook appears that he likes. The situation is too complex to be represented in advance, so every move produces consequences other than those intended. The designer, in Schön’s words, shapes the situation according to his initial appreciation of it; the situation “talks back”; and he responds to the back-talk. In good design, that conversation is reflective.

Three ideas from the chapter matter most for receivers. A frame is a way of setting the problem: deciding what to attend to and how to see it. A move is an action taken within the frame, which is also an experiment. Back-talk is what the situation does in response, including what nobody intended. When the back-talk cannot be absorbed within the frame, the practitioner can try a frame experiment: impose a new way of seeing and test it by acting on it.

At Ferrier House the receiver’s first frame is the one his repertoire supplies: a residential investment with management problems. Within that frame his moves are rent collection, compliance and a sale to a residential investor. The building talks back almost at once. The fire-safety findings, the open upper floors and the contractor’s unpaid subcontractors do not fit a management frame. By week three he has tried a second frame, a construction project in distress, and its moves are completely different: a fire engineer, a cost consultant, a decision on whether to complete. Neither frame is right. The instrument below lets you try four.

Instrument 31 · The frame experimentWhat does the building say back when you see it differently?

Choose a frame. The panel shows what that frame makes you attend to, the moves it suggests, and the back-talk Ferrier House gives in reply, including what the frame makes you miss. Compare frames; then choose “Hold two frames” to see Schön’s double vision at work.

Choose a frame

Start with the frame the receiver’s repertoire supplies: a residential investment with management problems.

Why this matters for a receiver

Receivers rarely fail for lack of technique. They fail by working skilfully within the wrong frame. Listening for back-talk, the things the building does that the frame did not predict, is how a receiver finds out that his frame is wrong while there is still time to change it.

Key terms
Frame
A way of setting a problem: what to attend to, and how to see it.
Move
An action within a frame, which is also an experiment.
Back-talk
The situation’s response to a move, including consequences nobody intended.
Frame experiment
Imposing a new frame on a situation and testing it by acting on it.
Cards · The conversation
17 · Rigour in practice

Three kinds of experiment: exploratory, move-testing and hypothesis-testing

In brief

Schön argued that practice has its own rigour, and that it is experimental, but not in the laboratory sense. He distinguished three kinds of on-the-spot experiment. Exploratory experiments ask “what if?” Move-testing experiments aim at a result and ask “do I like what I get?” Hypothesis-testing experiments discriminate between explanations. A receiver runs all three, often in the same week.

In the fifth chapter Schön gives the logic of experiment in practice. In its most generic sense, to experiment is to act in order to see what the action leads to. When action is undertaken only to see what follows, without predictions, it is an exploratory experiment: the probing, playful activity by which we get a feel for things. When we act to produce an intended change, as a carpenter fastens a board across a corner to stabilise it, the action is a move-testing experiment. In simple cases the move is affirmed if it works and negated if it does not. In complicated ones, moves produce effects beyond those intended, and the test is not only “do you get what you intend?” but “do you like what you get?” Finally, a hypothesis-testing experiment discriminates between competing explanations, as in science, though in practice only to the point at which a move is affirmed.

Practice also limits experiment. The practitioner cannot hold variables constant, and his experiments change the situation he is studying; he is, Schön says, in transaction with it. His remedy is a kind of rigour appropriate to practice: honest attention to the back-talk, a willingness to reframe, and the construction of “virtual worlds” (section 18) in which experiments can be run more cheaply than in the real one.

Instrument 32 · Sort the experimentsWhich kind of experiment is the receiver running?

Each action below was taken at Ferrier House. Decide whether it was exploratory, move-testing or hypothesis-testing. The explanation appears when you choose.

Why this matters for a receiver

Every move a receiver makes at Ferrier House is also an experiment, whether he treats it as one or not. Naming which kind (exploring, testing a move, testing a hypothesis) tells him what result to look for and when to stop.

Cards · Experiments
18 · Rehearsal

Virtual worlds: the cash-flow model, the sketch and the draft letter

In brief

Quist experiments on a sketchpad, not on the site. Schön calls the sketchpad a “virtual world”: a constructed representation of practice in which moves can be tried, slowed down, reversed and compared. Receivers have several: the cash-flow and exit model, the marked-up floor plan, the draft letter read aloud, the conversation rehearsed in the car. Their value is that they make experiment cheap. Their danger is that they are mistaken for the building.

Schön is explicit that the practitioner’s ability to construct and manipulate virtual worlds is a crucial part of his ability both to perform artistically and to experiment rigorously. In the virtual world some constraints of real practice can be relaxed: actions can be reversed, the pace can be slowed, and attention can be fixed on one variable at a time. The drawing reveals qualities and relations nobody imagined beforehand, which is why moves in it can function as experiments.

At Ferrier House the most important virtual world is the exit model the receiver builds in week five, comparing three courses: sell as it stands, complete floors six and seven and then sell, or complete and hold for a short period to stabilise lettings. In the model each course can be run a dozen times with different build costs, letting rates and yields, which the building itself would never allow. The model tells him something he did not expect: that the decision turns less on the build cost than on how long the completed flats would take to let.

The danger

Schön warns that virtual worlds work only if they are faithful to the real one in the respects that matter, and that the practitioner must remember what the representation leaves out. A cash-flow model leaves out the fourth-floor tenant. A floor plan leaves out the smell of damp. A draft letter leaves out the reader who will read it at midnight. Back-talk from the virtual world must always be checked against back-talk from the building.

Why this matters for a receiver

The exit model, the cash-flow forecast and the tabletop are the receiver’s virtual worlds: places to make mistakes cheaply. Their danger, as Stacey warns, is that they turn into defences against anxiety rather than rehearsal spaces.

Cards · Virtual worlds
19 · Commitment and openness

Double vision, and the constants a practitioner brings

In brief

Schön says the reflective practitioner must act on the frame he has chosen while knowing he can and must break it open later. He calls this “double vision”. It gets harder as an appointment goes on, because each move commits further and becomes less reversible. What keeps it possible, he argues, are relatively constant elements the practitioner brings: an overarching theory, an appreciative system and a role frame.

The passage on double vision is one of the best in the book. The inquirer must try to shape the situation to his frame, Schön writes, while holding himself open to the situation’s back-talk and willing to enter new confusions. He must act in accordance with the view he has adopted while recognising that he can always break it open later, indeed must, in order to make new sense of the situation. This becomes harder as the process continues: choices become more committing, moves more nearly irreversible, and, as the risk rises, so does the temptation to treat the view as the reality.

That describes month six at Ferrier House exactly. By then the receiver has committed to completing floors six and seven. A contractor has been appointed and a fire engineer has signed off a strategy. Then the contractor’s revised price arrives, nearly double the cost consultant’s estimate. Every instinct says to defend the commitment. Double vision says to treat the price as back-talk and to reopen the frame, even though reopening it costs time and face.

The constants

Schön lists what lets a practitioner keep his footing while frames shift. An overarching theory: a body of understanding broad enough to make sense of many situations (for a receiver, the law and economics of secured lending). An appreciative system: the values and preferences by which he judges whether a move’s outcome is good. A role frame: the way he understands his role, which shapes which problems he sets and which facts he treats as relevant. He also names the media, languages and repertoires the practitioner works in. The role frame matters most here. A receiver who frames his role as the lender’s enforcement agent sets different problems from one who frames it as the steward of an asset on behalf of several interests, and his reflection-in-action will be correspondingly narrower or wider.

Why this matters for a receiver

Most costly receivership decisions are commitments defended past the point where the back-talk said to reopen them. Double vision is the discipline of committing fully while keeping the frame open, and it depends on knowing which of one’s constants are actually constant.

Cards · Double vision
20 · Before the map

Schemata, frames and data: Bartlett, Klein’s data/frame theory, and Challoner’s schemata and tropes

In brief

Every cognitive map in the next section draws something that already exists before anyone draws it: a frame, or schema, through which the receiver reads the building. Bartlett showed in 1932 that people remember by reconstructing, bending what does not fit towards what they expect. Gary Klein’s data/frame theory turns this into a working account of sensemaking: people fit data into a frame and fit a frame around the data, and they elaborate, question, preserve, compare and replace frames as data arrive. John Challoner’s 2024 essay carries schemata upwards: beliefs assemble into personal and shared schemata, shared schemata aggregate into tropes, and tropes into culture, inside Margaret Archer’s morphogenetic cycle of structure, culture and agency. For a receiver the combination answers three questions: what frame am I reading this building through, what data has that frame made for me, and which of my frames are really the lender’s, or the profession’s?

Bartlett: schemata and the effort after meaning

Frederic Bartlett brought the idea of the schema, first used by Kant, into psychology in Remembering (1932). His best-known study asked English participants to read and later recall a Native American folk tale, “The War of the Ghosts”. With each recall the story became shorter, and details that did not fit the participants’ expectations were changed or dropped until it read like a familiar kind of story. Bartlett’s conclusion was that remembering is not retrieval but reconstruction: an effort after meaning in which new material is fitted to existing schemata, or schemata are built to hold it. Challoner adds a point that matters for any review. If one element of a schema is wrong, the schema does not simply carry an error; neighbouring elements are bent to stay consistent with it, and the distortion spreads.

At Ferrier House the schema was “finished residential investment”. It came from the file. It made the occupied floors the obvious place to start, made the mould in 4.06 look like a tenant matter, made the wedged fire doors a management lapse and made the open sixth and seventh floors “outstanding works”. Each reading was reasonable inside the schema, and each one made the others more plausible. That is Bartlett’s ripple: one wrong element, the word “finished”, bending five neighbours into line.

Klein’s data/frame theory

Gary Klein and his colleagues (Klein, Moon and Hoffman, 2006; Klein, Phillips, Rall and Peluso, 2007) built the data/frame theory from field studies of how experts, from fireground commanders to intelligence analysts, make sense of events. A frame is an explanatory structure that defines entities by their relationships to other entities. It can take the form of a story, a map, a script, a plan or a schema. The relation runs both ways: the data elicit and help to construct the frame, and the frame defines, connects and filters the data. Hence the theory’s definition: sensemaking is the process of fitting data into a frame and fitting a frame around the data. Neither comes first.

Several consequences follow, set out as assertions in the 2007 chapter and the Army Research Institute’s FOCUS report that tested them.

  • Data are constructed, not given. What counts as a datum, and what it means, depends on the frame. “Mould in 4.06” is a housekeeping complaint in one frame and evidence of water ingress in another.
  • Frames are set by anchors. The first one or two key data elements anchor the frame that is adopted, and that frame then guides the search for more data. At Ferrier House the anchors were the file’s “substantially complete” and a rent roll showing most flats paying.
  • Reasoning is abductive as well as deductive. People infer the best available explanation, then test it.
  • Sensemaking stops at congruence. When data and frame fit well enough to act, the search usually ends, which is efficient and also where errors hide.
  • Experts and novices reason the same way. The difference is the richer repertoire of frames experts carry, and their quicker detection of what does not fit. Klein’s claim is falsifiable: an expert who reliably “keeps an open mind” instead of working from a frame would count against it.
  • Understanding is functional. The aim is to know what to do, not only what is going on.
  • Mental models are fragmentary and assembled just in time. Experts carry many partial models and build the one they need on the spot, rather than holding one comprehensive picture.

The theory then names the activities by which frames change. Connecting or recognising a frame from the anchors. Elaborating it: filling slots, extending it, seeking data it predicts. Questioning it when an anomaly or a violated expectation appears. Preserving it by explaining the anomaly away, which is often right (not every oddity matters) and sometimes fixation. Comparing two or more frames against the same data. Seeking a new frame and reframing: replacing the frame, at which point discarded data are recovered and old data reread. The theory also links backward-looking sensemaking, which explains what happened, to forward-looking mental simulation, which projects what will happen next. That is the bridge to Klein’s recognition-primed decision model (section 06).

Read against the rest of this treatise, the data/frame theory gives Schön’s “frame” a mechanism. Schön’s back-talk is data that will not fit; his reframing is Klein’s reframing; his double vision is the discipline of holding a frame while watching for the data that would question it. It also explains Rudolph’s four modes (section 10): fixating is preserving too long, vagabonding is comparing without committing, and adapting is elaborating a frame while keeping a second one alive. And it says why the xAAR’s third question, “what caused the difference?”, is so hard. The answer has to be found inside the frame that caused the difference.

Challoner: beliefs, schemata, tropes and culture

John Challoner’s essay “A Deep Dive into Beliefs, Schemata, Tropes and Culture” (2024) builds upwards from information to culture. He treats information as physical (after Landauer) and reproducible, translatable and transmissible, so that beliefs, schemata and tropes are copies of information whose accuracy can degrade with each reproduction. Beliefs are acquired empirically, by observing physical and social reality, or socially, by socialisation and imitation; the more processed a belief, the less likely it is to be true. Beliefs and practices form and revise schemata, and schemata in turn generate beliefs and behaviour.

Three of his claims bear directly on a receiver.

  • Schemata are not transmitted whole. Only their components travel, as beliefs, stories and behaviour, and each recipient reassembles them into a schema of their own. A receiver cannot hand his frame to the relationship manager; she will rebuild it from his report, inside hers.
  • Dissonance can come from below awareness. Extending Festinger, Challoner argues that dissonance can arise between a conscious belief and a subconscious schema, or between two subconscious schemata, so that people feel discomfort without being able to say why. He presents this as an original contribution. Implicit-cognition research has long studied related conflicts, so it is better read as a useful emphasis than as a new discovery. The receiver’s unease in week four, before he could name the problem, fits it well.
  • Schemata change slowly, and then all at once. New information is first assimilated by reinterpreting it to fit. As anomalies accumulate the schema destabilises into a hybrid, old framework and new insight coexisting uneasily, and finally accommodation produces a new schema. Challoner draws the parallel with Kuhn’s paradigm shifts, the difference being that paradigms are consciously held and schemata usually are not.

When similar schemata are shared across many people they form a trope: an emergent, higher-order pattern which, like a shoal to a fish, is made of its members and shapes them in turn. Several tropes together make a culture. In his Figure 3, reality (events, states and relationships, including other people and their beliefs) feeds individuals by observation; their beliefs and practices form personal and shared schemata; shared schemata aggregate into tropes and tropes into culture; and culture disaggregates back into the schemata that generate behaviour. Tropes change incrementally, by replacement, or by merging; and they change because of external shifts, internal contradictions, or people deliberately challenging them. Challoner distinguishes adaptive social change, which refines a trope from within, from transformative change, which replaces it.

He sets all of this inside a modified version of Margaret Archer’s morphogenetic cycle. Society gives agents roles (structure) and cultural demands (values, norms and beliefs). Agents either accept them without much thought (automaticity, which affirms culture and structure) or, if dissatisfied, turn to reflexivity, look for alternatives and promote them (enculturement and structural change). Challoner adds the natural environment as a co-evolving element, and nests agency: individuals, families, groups, organisations and nations each run the same cycle at their own level.

Receivership has its tropes. “The lender wants a number.” “The receiver is the bank’s agent.” “The valuation on the file is the starting point.” “Agents know their buildings.” None was invented by anyone at Ferrier House; each was reassembled there, in many heads, from the profession and the lender’s credit culture. The week-three £6m was a receiver’s belief shaped by the trope that credit papers carry single figures. The credit committee’s rule that early figures are provisional is the same trope being changed from inside: adaptive change, prompted by an anomaly and carried by one reflexive conversation.

Reading the three together

Bartlett explains why a wrong frame spreads, Klein explains how frames are worked on in the moment, and Challoner explains where frames come from and how they travel between people and up into culture. The receiver’s practical questions follow. What are my anchors, and when did I set them? What data has my frame created, and what has it hidden? What have I explained away, and how many times? Which frame would the lender, the agent or the residents use, and would it read the same data differently? And which of my frames are not mine at all, but tropes of the profession or of this lender that I have reassembled without noticing? The next section draws these frames as maps; the instruments below let you work them first.

Instrument 33 · The data/frame workbenchWhich frame did the data fit, and what did the frame do to the data?

Twelve pieces of data reach the receiver in the first five weeks at Ferrier House. Three frames compete to explain them: a finished residential investment, a part-built project in distress and a live safety case. Choose the frame you are working in, then press Next datum. For each one, choose what to do with it, using Klein’s activities: elaborate the frame, preserve it by explaining the datum away, question it, compare frames, or reframe. The bars show how well each frame fits everything seen so far; the explained-away counter shows the load you are carrying; the panel shows how the datum reads under each frame (the frame constructs the data), and what the receiver actually did. Switch to The receiver’s path to replay the real sequence.

Instrument 34 · From reality to culture, and backHow did a belief about one building become a rule in a credit culture?

Challoner’s Figure 3, redrawn for Ferrier House. On the left, reality: events, states and relationships. In the middle, two individuals, the receiver and the lender’s relationship manager, each with beliefs and practices, personal schemata and shared schemata. On the right, tropes and the culture they aggregate into. Choose a trace and step through it with Next: each step lights the path the belief takes and explains it.
