Why this matters for a receiver

A receiver is paid to read buildings, and he reads them through frames he mostly did not choose. Naming the anchors, logging what has been explained away, and asking which frame the lender or the residents would use turns sensemaking from something that happens to him into something he can review. And because frames travel only as beliefs and behaviour, the first report is not a description the lender receives intact: it is material from which the lender builds its own frame. Write it as frame and data, with what would change your mind.

Cards · Frames and schemata
21 · Mapping the mind at work

Cognitive mapping: drawing the frames a receiver thinks with

In brief

Schön’s frames are hard to reflect on because they are invisible to the person using them. Cognitive mapping makes them visible. The tradition runs from Edward Tolman’s rats in 1948, through George Kelly’s personal constructs and Robert Axelrod’s causal maps of political elites, to Colin Eden and Fran Ackermann’s cognitive mapping and SODA method, Anne Huff’s maps of strategic thought and Bart Kosko’s fuzzy cognitive maps. For a receiver it offers two things reflection alone cannot: a picture of his own reasoning that he can check, and a way of putting several people’s reasoning side by side. The second is the I/we split drawn on paper.

Maps as frames made visible

Every map in this section is an attempt to draw a frame, in Klein’s sense, or a schema, in Bartlett’s and Challoner’s (section 20). Seeing them that way changes how each method should be used. Tolman’s strip map is a frame with too few anchors; his comprehensive map is a repertoire of frames. Kelly’s repertory grid elicits the constructs a frame is built from. A causal map draws the frame’s slots and the links between them, so it shows where the frame will predict data and where it will be blind. Eden and Ackermann’s merged group map is the closest thing to a picture of a shared schema in formation, and, if it outlives the project, of a trope. A fuzzy cognitive map runs a frame forward: it is Klein’s mental simulation made explicit.

Three consequences follow for practice. First, a map elicited after the event is a reconstruction (Bartlett), so it shows the frame as remembered, tidied by hindsight; maps drawn at the time, or anchored in dated documents, are more honest. Second, a map records one frame and hides the data that frame explained away, so ask for the explained-away log beside it: which anomalies did this map have no node for? Third, because schemata travel only in pieces, a merged map is not three frames added together; each party rebuilds the group map inside its own schema. The workshop’s real product is the conversation in which the pieces were exchanged, which is Eden’s own caution that maps are tools for talking, not pictures of minds.

The critics bear on all of this. Eden warns that maps model what people say, for a purpose. Hodgkinson and colleagues show that different elicitation methods yield different maps. Weick and Stacey would add that the frame lives in the organising and the relating more than in any head. And Kaplan’s framing contests are a reminder that when maps disagree, the one that prevails may be the one with the most powerful sponsor, not the best fit to the data.

Tolman: strip maps and comprehensive maps

Edward Tolman’s paper “Cognitive maps in rats and men” (1948) argued that rats in mazes learned not just sequences of turns but something like a map of the environment, which let them take new routes when the familiar one was blocked. He distinguished narrow, strip-like maps from broad, comprehensive ones, and suggested that the difference shows only when the environment changes. At the close of the paper he turned to people, and argued that strong motivation or intense frustration narrows the map. A receiver under time pressure in week one works with a strip map: rent, deposits, sale. Ferrier House changed the maze. Reflection is the work of widening the map.

Kelly: personal constructs

George Kelly’s personal construct theory (1955) treats each person as a kind of scientist who construes the world through bipolar constructs: dimensions such as “cooperative versus obstructive” or “a number versus a hope”. His repertory grid elicits them by showing three elements (people, situations, buildings) and asking in what way two are alike and different from the third. The answer is a construct, with its own opposite. The elements are then rated on every construct, giving a map of how that person differentiates his world. Laddering (asking “why does that matter?”) moves up to superordinate constructs; pyramiding (asking “how would I know?”) moves down to behavioural cues. A grid run on a receiver’s past appointments surfaces the constructs his tacit judgement uses, and often a few he did not know he had.

Axelrod and Huff: causal maps

Robert Axelrod’s Structure of Decision (1976) defined a cognitive map as a graphic representation intended to capture the structure of a decision maker’s stated beliefs about a particular problem: concepts as points, beliefs about causes as signed arrows. His contributors mapped the British Eastern Committee in 1918 and the Constitutional Convention. Anne Huff’s Mapping Strategic Thought (1990) carried the method into strategic management, and Fiol and Huff (1992) argued that managers need a portfolio of maps (of identity, of categories and of causes) to act. Weick and Bougon described maps as letting people perceive environments beyond the range of immediate perception.

Eden and Ackermann: cognitive mapping and SODA

Colin Eden’s cognitive mapping, developed from the late 1970s and set out in the European Journal of Operational Research in 1988, is founded on Kelly. A map is built from the client’s own words, each concept written where possible as a bipolar statement with its contrasting pole (“complete floors six and seven … rather than sell as a shell”), linked by arrows meaning “may lead to”. Goals sit at the top, options at the bottom, and the strategic issues in between. Eden and Ackermann’s Strategic Options Development and Analysis (SODA) takes individual maps from interviews, checks them with each interviewee, and merges them into a group map, used to negotiate goals, issues and options. Because the map uses the problem owners’ own language, they own it; and because it is formally constructed, it can be analysed for central concepts, clusters and feedback loops.

That merging step is the I/we split in another form. Each person’s individual map is his own; the group map belongs to the team; and the differences between them are where the learning is. Mapping the lender’s, receiver’s and agent’s understandings of Ferrier House separately in week two would have shown, on one sheet, that the three parties were working with three different problems.

Kosko and Novak: maps that move, maps that teach

Bart Kosko’s fuzzy cognitive maps (1986) extended Axelrod’s maps by giving each causal link a weight and letting the map run: concepts activate one another through the weighted arrows, feedback loops included, until the pattern settles. They are a cheap way to see what a set of beliefs implies over time, a virtual world in Schön’s sense. Joseph Novak’s concept maps, built on David Ausubel’s theory of meaningful learning, link concepts with labelled propositions and prize cross-links between distant parts of a map, which Novak saw as the creative leaps of new knowledge. Peter Senge called the underlying objects mental models and warned that, left unexamined, they keep people seeing what they have always seen.

Instrument 35 · Three maps of Ferrier House, and the group mapWhat did each party believe causes what, and where did their maps disagree?

Each map is drawn in the Eden style from week two: goals at the top, options at the bottom, arrows meaning “may lead to” (solid for “more of this means more of that”, dashed for “less”). Choose the receiver’s, the relationship manager’s or the agent’s map (the I maps), or merge them into the SODA group map (the we map). In the group map, concepts held by only one party are marked; conflicts are red. Then switch to “Completion” to see how the receiver’s own map changed by month eleven. Select any concept to see who holds it and what it led to.

Select a map, then a concept.

Instrument 36 · A repertory grid on six appointmentsHow does the receiver tell one building from another?

Kelly’s triadic method. Each round shows three of the receiver’s past appointments. Choose which one is the odd one out; the construct it elicits is revealed, with its opposite. As constructs accumulate, the grid fills with ratings (1 = left pole, 5 = right pole) and the panel reports which constructs move together, a sign of a deeper construct the receiver may not have named. Ferrier House is the sixth element.

Instrument 37 · A fuzzy cognitive map of the exitWhat do the receiver’s beliefs imply, if he lets them run?

Kosko’s method. Each arrow carries a weight between −1 and +1. Set the starting conditions (how far completion is pursued, how fast the agent answers repairs, how early whole-block buyers are tested), then run the map. Concepts pass activation along the arrows, feedback included, for twelve steps. Watch where it settles. Change one belief (for instance, the weight from letting time to net recovery) and run it again: this is the week-five surprise, reproduced.

The limits of maps

A map is a representation of stated beliefs, not of cognition itself; Eden says plainly that the model is not intended as a transparent picture of thought. Maps capture what people can say, which is the relational layer of tacit knowledge, and miss the somatic and collective layers. And maps can be gamed: in a meeting with the lender, a receiver may draw the map he thinks he ought to have. Used privately for the I ledger, and in a facilitated SODA-style session for the we ledger, they are among the most powerful reflective tools there are.

Why this matters for a receiver

Reflection asks a practitioner to examine his frames. Mapping gives him something to examine. A receiver who maps his reasoning in week two and again at completion can see, on paper, how his understanding of the building changed, which is the most direct evidence of learning there is.

Cards · Cognitive mapping
22 · The after action review

The After Action Review: from the National Training Center to the boardroom

In brief

The After Action Review began in the US Army in the mid-1970s, as part of training soldiers through realistic engagement simulation. It replaced the instructor’s “critique” with a discussion among the people who did the work, run against performance standards, in a non-punitive atmosphere. It rests on a handful of questions, beginning with “what was supposed to happen?”. It is now used by health systems, fire services, oil companies, software teams and intelligence agencies. For a receiver it is the obvious way to turn reflection-on-action into shared learning.

The US Army Research Institute’s history of the method, by Morrison and Meliza (1999), dates the first AAR methods to the mid-1970s. They came out of ARI work on training through engagement simulation (the REALTRAIN programme), where units fought each other with laser-based weapons and then had to make sense of what had happened. Before that, the standard tool was the “performance critique”, in which an instructor or umpire told a unit what it had done wrong. The AAR inverted the authority. The facilitator asked questions; the soldiers worked out the answers. The method matured at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California, where units fight a permanent, highly skilled opposing force and are reviewed after every engagement.

The Army’s training circular TC 25-20 defines the AAR as a professional discussion of an event, focused on performance standards, that enables soldiers to discover for themselves what happened, why it happened, and how to sustain strengths and improve on weaknesses. The circular insists on an objective and non-punitive atmosphere. It is not a critique and not a grading exercise.

The four questions

Most versions reduce the review to four questions. What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we sustain, and what will we improve, next time? The order matters. A debrief usually starts with what happened; an AAR starts with the intention, so that the gap between intention and outcome becomes the object of inquiry. A post-mortem usually looks for causes and makes recommendations for others; an AAR concentrates on the participants’ own actions and on what they themselves will do.

Knowledge-management writers carried the method into business in the 1990s. At BP, Chris Collison and Geoff Parcell built a learning cycle of three tools: the peer assist (learning before doing), the AAR (learning while doing, after each step) and the retrospect (learning after doing, at the end of a project). The UK Overseas Development Institute and NASA both published guides drawing on their account. The World Health Organization published its own AAR guidance in 2019, and in 2020 adapted it into an intra-action review for countries still in the middle of the COVID-19 response. The intra-action review is the AAR moved inside Schön’s action-present.

Where receivership fits

A receivership has natural review points: the end of the first fortnight, each quarterly report, each major decision (complete or sell as is), the exchange of contracts, and completion. A short AAR at each of the early points is an intra-action review: it can still change the outcome. The review at completion is a retrospect: it changes the next appointment.

Why this matters for a receiver

Receivers already reflect, but usually alone and usually after the event. The AAR gives that reflection a shared, disciplined form that a lender, a receiver and a managing agent can run together in an hour.

Cards · The AAR
23 · What the research says

Does it work? The evidence on debriefs and AARs

In brief

Unusually for a management technique, the AAR has a strong evidence base. Two meta-analyses find that properly run debriefs improve performance substantially: by about 25 per cent on average in one, with an even larger effect in the other. The gains depend on how the review is run. Alignment with the task, structure, good facilitation and objective evidence of what happened all help. Reviewing successes as well as failures helps too.

Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013) pooled 46 samples covering 2,136 participants. Debriefs improved effectiveness by about 25 per cent on average, an effect size of d = 0.67. The effect was similar for teams and individuals, and for real and simulated work. Debriefs worked better when they were aligned with the purpose of the work, facilitated, and structured. Keiser and Arthur’s later meta-analyses (2021, 2022) covered 61 studies and found an overall effect of d = 0.79. They identified alignment and the use of objective records of performance as important moderators, and found that facilitation interacts with other features rather than working on its own.

Ellis and Davidi (2005) studied Israeli soldiers in navigation training. Those debriefed on both their successes and their failures improved more than those debriefed on failures alone, and they built richer mental models of the task. The point has direct consequences for receivers, whose reviews (when they happen at all) are usually triggered by a loss.

Instrument 38 · The evidence, drawnHow big is the effect, and what makes it bigger?

The left panel shows the two pooled effect sizes as the overlap between a reviewed and an unreviewed group: the further the curves separate, the larger the effect. On the right, switch on the design features of a review and watch the indicative strength of a receivership AAR change. The right-hand panel is illustrative, not a statistical model.

Design features

The limits

The studies are mostly of military, medical and training teams doing repeated tasks with fast feedback. A receivership is a one-off, long-cycle piece of work in which the result (the sale price) arrives months after the decisions that shaped it. The evidence supports reviewing; it does not tell us how large the effect will be in receivership. Darling, Parry and Moore warned in 2005 that AARs often identify past mistakes without improving future performance, and Peter Senge warned that organisations reduce the living practice of AARs to a sterile technique. Both warnings are taken up in sections 28 and 41.

Why this matters for a receiver

The evidence says reviews help, by roughly a quarter on average, and help most when they are structured, honest and followed by action. For a receiver that is a reason to hold them, and a warning that a review without follow-up is mostly ritual.

24 · The method behind the review

The Five Elements method in full: where the xAAR lives

In brief

The xAAR is the last step of a five-phase method, and it makes full sense only inside it. Each phase asks its own questions and stores its own records in a shared repository. The method is recursive: any issue that arises mid-session can be opened as a “child” session with the issue as its Purpose, then closed back into its “parent”. A session can last seconds, as a real-time checklist, or years. That range is exactly Schön’s range of action-presents, and it is why the Five Elements serve reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action alike.

In the third part of his 2016 series Graves sets the method out phase by phase. Purpose (forming; why) asks what question the session should address, its context and scope, and what outcomes and indicators of success are expected; it starts with “the problem” and applies Five Whys or an equivalent to find why it matters, what happens if it is or is not addressed, and how it fits the larger shared enterprise. People (storming; who) identifies the stakeholders, each one’s stake in the question, their “response-abilities” (using RACI, SEMPER or similar, including whether power is exercised with or against others), how to engage them, the story that would unite them, and how to resolve conflicts that exist or are likely. Preparation (norming; how) asks what must be in place before acting, and what constraints of time, budget, people, risk appetite and emergence set “just enough detail”; it uses judgement, supported by guidelines, to select assessment, sensemaking and design tools, and defines the conditions at which just enough detail has been reached and just enough action may begin. Process (performing; where, when, with what) follows the plan, records outcomes on action records and metrics, and reassesses on the fly with tools such as OODA and SCAN. Performance (adjourning; success) closes the session: what was achieved, what benefits were realised relative to the layered purpose, what lessons were learned. Here, optionally, comes the xAAR.

Each phase ends with a bracketed instruction to store something in the repository: discussion notes and initial requests for Purpose; stakeholder lists, RACI maps and engagement plans for People; plans, models, action-record templates and metrics for Preparation; action records, metrics and run-time reassessments for Process; and AAR records, questions, commitments and amended action records for Performance. The xAAR’s repository step is not an afterthought. It closes a chain of records that began with the first question.

Fractal, nested and non-linear

Graves is explicit that the pattern is recursive and fractal. At any point a practitioner may identify an issue that needs addressing on its own terms, store the status of the current session, open a new session with the issue as its Purpose, and return to the parent when the child is complete. He may jump back to an earlier phase. He should not jump forward without returning to complete what was skipped; in particular, he warns, skipping the People phase almost always causes worse storming later. Sessions may be nested to any depth and interrupted at any point, so the practitioner must keep track of the status of each one.

On duration Graves is equally clear. At its most minimal a session may last seconds, with the Five Elements tag-lines used as a real-time checklist; at its largest it may be a multi-year programme containing many nested child sessions. Neither duration nor complexity is built into the pattern. They come from how it is used. Put beside Schön, this is the same insight as the action-present: the shape of reflective inquiry stays the same whether the window is a corridor conversation or a six-month exit decision.

At Ferrier House

The appointment is the parent session; its Purpose is to realise the security at the best price reasonably obtainable while keeping the building safe and lawful. The missing fire-door closers on day four open a child session with its own Purpose (make the stairs safe tonight), its own People (agent, fire engineer, residents of floors five to seven), its own Preparation, Process and Performance, and its own short review, closed within forty-eight hours. The mould in flat 4.06 opens another. The complete-or-sell decision is a child session that runs for five months and has children of its own. The final xAAR reviews the parent, drawing on the repository records of every child.

Instrument 39 · Nested sessions at Ferrier HouseWhich session are you in, and what has it stored?

The outer ring is the appointment. Each inner ring is a child session opened when a surprise arrived, with its own five phases. Select a session to see its Purpose, its duration and what it stored at each phase. Turn on “skip People” to see what Graves warns will happen.

Select a session.

Why this matters for a receiver

A receivership is not one decision but a nest of them, opened as surprises arrive. Treating each surprise as a child session, with its own purpose, people and short review, keeps the parent appointment’s record coherent and gives the final xAAR something to review besides memory.

Cards · Five Elements
25 · The Tetradian toolkit, redrawn

Tom Graves’s diagrams: Five Elements, SCAN, the task, the review and the seven sins

In brief

The xAAR is one piece of a connected toolkit that Graves has built over two decades on his Tetradian weblog. Five Elements gives the cycle the review sits in. SCAN gives the sensemaking frame and the time axis that places review “after action”. The structure of a task gives the box every piece of work, a receivership included, should have, with review built in. His continuous-learning practice gives the review its timings and its three rules. And his seven sins of dubious discipline name the ways sensemaking goes wrong. All six are redrawn below, interactively, for Ferrier House.

Five Elements: a cycle, five lenses and two overlays

Graves built Five Elements in 2012 as a metaframework. The base frame is Tuckman’s group dynamics (forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning), turned from a line into a cycle so that adjourning feeds the next forming. Over it he laid the classical Chinese wu xing, about which he had written in his 1978 book Needles of Stone, and Nigel Green and Carl Bate’s VPEC-T (Values, Policies, Events, Content, Trust), which he reworked, explicitly as a non-standard use, into labels for the transitions between phases. In the post only two transition labels are given in the text: Values between Purpose and People, and Completions between Process and Performance; the others appear only in his graphic, and are not reproduced here. He also cross-mapped five effectiveness qualities to the elements: Appropriate (Purpose), Elegant (People), Efficient (Preparation), Reliable (Process) and Integrated (Performance). He insists the elements are lenses for viewing activities, not fixed categories of work, and that each can be applied recursively within itself.

SCAN: certainty, time and the edges between

SCAN, the subject of Treatise VIII, maps sensemaking and decision-making on two axes. Horizontally runs a scale from absolute certainty to infinite uncertainty, crossed somewhere by the boundary of effective certainty. Vertically runs the time available before action must be taken, down to “NOW!”. The four regions are Simple, Complicated, Ambiguous and Not-known. Graves later named the edges: the edge of action (Simple–Complicated), renamed the edge of commitment; the edge of uncertainty (Complicated–Ambiguous); the edge of innovation (Ambiguous–Not-known); and the edge of panic (Simple–Not-known). In a 2018 reframe he relabelled the vertical regions Before, During and After, and argued that the full OODA loop (which he prefers to read as Sense, Make-sense, Decide, Act) must include time after the action to sense what has happened, a region he says maps closely to the Performance phase of Five Elements. That is where the xAAR lives.

Graves also warns against confusing loops. The “Act” in OODA aligns with the “Do” in Deming’s PDCA; the “Act” in PDCA is better read as “Adjust”, because it changes the underpinnings. A receiver’s review is a PDCA “Act” in that sense: it adjusts how the next appointment will be run.

The structure of a task

In 2021 Graves set out the structure every task should have: Context (purpose, vision, values, laws and standards, success criteria), Scope (boundaries, stakeholders, requirements), Plan (building the plan, with work-instructions, preventive checks, emergency checks and guidelines for unprecedented events; then setup for action), Action (work-instructions for the predictable part, handling of variances and exceptions, and records of what happened), and Review. Review has three parts: benefits-realised (did we achieve what we set out to do?), lessons-learned (the five xAAR questions, with “what can I do better next time?” as individual responsibility and “what can we do better next time?” as collective responsibility), and tasks-arising (registering what follows). Tasks nest to any depth; every task keeps a trail of provenance back to purpose and a trail of derivation recording where new tasks came from.

The review’s timings and rules

In his 2017 talk on building continuous learning into practice, Graves gives the AAR five precursors (why, who, how, what, outcomes). He also suggests how to divide the review time. About 10 per cent goes on what was supposed to happen and 10 per cent on what actually happened. About 20 per cent goes on the sources of difference, including what worked unexpectedly well. And 20 to 30 per cent goes on each of the I and the we, each ending in a commitment. Over half the time, in other words, goes on the two learning questions. He gives three rules: aim to learn how to do it better; pin your stripes at the door (everyone has equal response-ability in the room, whatever their rank); and no blame.

The seven sins of dubious discipline

In a 2015 series Graves named seven common ways sensemaking discipline fails: the Hype Hubris, the Golden-Age Game, the Newage Nuisance, the Meaning Mistake, the Possession Problem, the Reality Risk, and getting Lost in the Learning Labyrinth. In his inventory of tools he places the xAAR alongside effectiveness-mapping and the seven sins in the Performance phase: the review checks results, and the sins check the thinking that produced them. The readings of each sin for receivership in the instrument below are this treatise’s.

Instrument 40 · The Graves atlas, for Ferrier HouseSix diagrams, one appointment

In SCAN, the six surprises are plotted and can be moved through Before, During and After. In the task, follow the trails. In the review budget, set the length of the meeting. Why this matters for a receiver

Graves gives the receiver a vocabulary for the whole appointment, not just its end: sessions within sessions, each with its own purpose, people, preparation, process and performance, and a review budget that puts most of the time on the I and the we.

26 · The extended review

Graves’s extended After Action Review: five questions round the Five Elements

In brief

Tom Graves, the enterprise architect behind the SCAN framework (Treatise VIII), extended the AAR in 2016 by mapping its questions onto his Five Elements cycle of Purpose, People, Preparation, Process and Performance. He made three changes. He split the learning question into “what can I learn?” and “what can we learn?”. He named the outputs. And he required the records to be kept in a repository. The image below is Graves’s own drawing of it: five pentagons around a centre marked “Trust / Commitment”. His other Five Elements diagrams put trust in a second place as well, on the transition that closes one cycle and opens the next; the subsection “Graves on Tuckman, and where trust and commitment sit” below sets the two side by side.

Graves sets out the xAAR in the third part of his 2016 series Towards a whole-enterprise architecture standard. His core method runs through five phases named after the classical Chinese Five Elements and paired with Tuckman’s stages of group development. Purpose (forming: why) identifies the reason and scope for the work. People (storming: who) deals with the people issues. Preparation (norming: how) prepares for action. Process (performing: where, when, with what) enacts it. Performance (adjourning: success) closes the session and prepares for the next. The xAAR is an optional tool applied within the fifth phase, and it walks the five questions back round the whole cycle:

  • What was supposed to happen? maps to Preparation: the plan, the model, the assumptions.
  • What actually happened? maps to Process: the action as it was enacted.
  • What was the source of any difference? maps to Performance: the gap between intention and result.
  • What can I learn from this, to do differently next time? maps to Purpose: the individual’s why.
  • What can we learn from this, to do differently next time? maps to People: the shared who.

The outputs are named. Graves lists questions to be addressed in future sessions; personal commitments to change, or skills to develop; collective commitments to change, or shared skills to develop; and information and insights to be passed on for wider situational awareness. The records (AAR records, questions, commitments, amendments to action records and metrics) go into a repository, so that the next cycle starts from what this one learned. In his later post on the structure of a task (2021), the same pair of questions reappears as “what can I do better next time?” and “what can we do better next time?”, inside a review of benefits realised, lessons learned and tasks arising.

A second reading: the five elements as lenses

The Five Elements can also be read as five lenses for the whole review, rather than as five slots for five questions. On this reading Purpose re-examines whether the original question and intended outcome were still the right ones; People reviews stakeholders, collaboration, trust and commitments; Preparation tests the plans, models and assumptions; Process examines what actually happened, including the surprises; and Performance captures lessons, benefits (direct and indirect, including costs avoided) and new questions for the next cycle. The two readings are compatible. Graves’s own text gives the question mapping; the lens reading is a useful way to run the review in practice, and the instrument below shows both. The mention of costs avoided belongs to the lens reading rather than to Graves’s 2016 post.

Do not rehearse the review

Patricia Shaw’s story of two colleagues who rehearsed their contribution to an open meeting (section 11) is a warning for the xAAR. If the lender and the receiver agree the narrative beforehand, the room will sense it, trust will become the topic, and nothing will be learned. Prepare the records; do not prepare the conversation. And keep the ledgers as commitments and questions, not a method: Preben Friis’s improvisation course got worse each year after he wrote it down as a nine-step manual.

Maps in the review

The xAAR works best with the cognitive maps of section 21 on the table. The answer to “what was supposed to happen?” is each party’s week-two map; the answer to “what caused the difference?” is often a single arrow that was wrong, or missing. The I question compares each person’s week-two map with his completion map. The we question compares the merged group map with the reality, and asks which concepts only one party held. Graves’s own suggested timings (section 25) give more than half the meeting to the I and the we.

Graves on Tuckman, and where trust and commitment sit in his diagrams

The xAAR only makes sense against the cycle it is drawn on. Graves says he has used the Five Elements since before 1978, when he wrote about classic Five Element theory in Needles of Stone, and that it is a merge of Tuckman’s group dynamics with the Chinese wu xing. The mapping is one to one: Purpose is forming, People is storming, Preparation is norming, Process is performing, and Performance is adjourning. Each element also has an effectiveness theme: appropriate, elegant, efficient, reliable and integrated. Graves made two changes to Tuckman. He turned the line into a cycle, so that the adjourning of one project links to the forming of the next. And he treats the five phases as lenses that apply recursively, at any scale from a five-minute task to a programme.

He is insistent that the whole cycle must be run in order. His failure modes are telling for trust. Skip People and go straight to planning, or jump from Why to What, and in both cases his slide is marked “Storming!”: the storm you avoided comes back later, at a worse time. In Tuckman’s terms, storming is where a group discovers whether disagreement is safe, so a skipped storm is trust left untested.

Trust and commitment then appear in two places in Graves’s diagrams. The first is the transitions. Borrowing Nigel Green’s VPEC-T and skewing it half a step, Graves reads its terms as the links between phases: Values from Purpose to People, Policies from People to Preparation, Events from Preparation to Process, and Completions (his replacement for “Content”) from Process to Performance. On his service-cycle slides the remaining link, from Performance back to Purpose, is labelled Trust / Commitment, beside the words “start here”. In the service cycle trust is, in his phrase, a measure of match to shared aspirations. It frames the cycle before any transaction (trust, values, policies), is put to work during it (policies, events, completions), and is reaffirmed afterwards (completions, trust). His warning follows: skip the completions and there is no reaffirmation of mutual trust, and trust in the market slowly deteriorates.

The second place is the centre of his xAAR drawing, shown above: five questions round the pentagon, and “Trust / Commitment” in the middle, behind all of them. The two placements are consistent. In the service cycle, trust is what each completed cycle reaffirms and what the next one starts from; in the review, trust and commitment are the conditions of every question. Graves’s 2014 post on product, service and trust says trust is at the centre of everything in any enterprise, takes a great deal of work to build, very little to lose, and is broken fastest by perceived betrayal. (The green dashed lines between the pentagons in the xAAR drawing sit exactly where his transitions sit in the other diagrams; reading them as transitions is this treatise’s interpretation, not his stated one.)

For a receiver this gives a simple test of any appointment. Was each phase completed, or skipped? Were the completions acknowledged, to the lender, the agent and the residents, so that trust was reaffirmed? And did the xAAR end in commitments, the other half of the centre, with owners and dates? The Graves atlas in section 25 now labels all five transitions, and the reversible trust and commitment card below sets Graves beside Edmondson, Tuckman, chaos, complexity, chaordic practice and high-reliability organising.

Graves sources: Perils of prior-art (2011) · Metaframeworks, Part 3 (2012) · Not quite VPEC-T (2010) · Metaframeworks, Part 5 (2012) · Product, service and trust (2014) · Whole-enterprise architecture slides (2016) · Continuous-learning slides (2017)

      Why trust and commitment sit at the centre

      Why this matters for a receiver

      The xAAR turns the end of an appointment into two sets of commitments with owners and dates: the receiver’s own and the team’s. Kept apart, neither can be blamed on the other and neither can be quietly dropped.

      Cards · The xAAR
      27 · The split that matters most

      The I and the we: two learnings, two commitments, two records

      In brief

      The part of the xAAR that matters most for receivership work is the split between “what can I learn?” and “what can we learn?”. A receiver’s own learning and the shared learning of the lender, the receiver and the agent are separate commitments. They have different owners, different authority behind them and different ways of failing. The review should record each, separately, and neither should be allowed to stand in for the other.

      Most reviews collapse the two. In a standard AAR the last question is “what will we do differently?”, and in a meeting of three organisations “we” quietly becomes nobody. Each party leaves believing the lesson belongs to the others. The lender thinks the receiver will change his first-week checklist. The receiver thinks the lender will change how it describes buildings in its instructions. The agent thinks both will tell it earlier. Six months later, at the next appointment, nothing has changed, because no one person committed to anything.

      The opposite failure is quieter. Everyone records personal resolutions, and the relationship itself learns nothing. The receiver resolves to walk the upper floors on day one. The relationship manager resolves to read the monitoring surveyor’s reports more carefully. Nobody notices that the real failure at Ferrier House was a joint one: the instruction letter, the receiver’s acceptance and the agent’s handover were three documents that never met, and no individual resolution will fix that.

      Why the commitments differ

      They differ first in who can keep them. An I commitment is within the power of the person who makes it. The receiver can change his own first-day routine tomorrow without asking anyone. A we commitment depends on several parties, none of whom can deliver it alone: a joint first-fortnight protocol needs the lender to change its instruction letter, the receiver to change his acceptance, and the agent to change its handover.

      They differ in the authority behind them. The receiver’s duties are personal. He owes the mortgagor and others interested in the equity of redemption a duty of good faith, and a duty of reasonable care as to price on sale. Those duties cannot be delegated to a team, and his learning about how to discharge them is his own. Schön’s reflection-in-action is likewise individual: it happens inside one practitioner’s action-present. The team’s learning, by contrast, belongs to the relationship. It lives in shared documents, shared timetables and shared expectations, and it outlasts any one appointment.

      They differ in how they fail. I commitments fail through over-learning: the resolution fades into the repertoire and is forgotten. We commitments fail through diffusion: each party assumes another has the action. The remedies differ too. The I ledger needs private review: the receiver’s own notebook, his supervision or mentoring, his CPD reflection. The we ledger needs a named owner for each item, a date, and a place in the next joint meeting’s agenda.

      Different kinds of learning

      The split also corresponds to a distinction Argyris and Schön drew between individual and organisational learning (section 31). An individual can learn without the organisation learning: a receiver can become wiser while the lender’s panel arrangements stay exactly as they were. And an organisation can learn in ways no individual intended: a revised instruction template can change every future appointment whether or not anyone remembers why. Schön’s chapter on the art of managing describes an organisation’s learning system as “dynamically conservative”: it works to keep things as they are. The we ledger is the means of getting a lesson past that conservatism.

      Instrument 43 · Sort the lessons into I and weWhose commitment is this, and who can keep it?

      These are lessons from the Ferrier House review. Decide whether each is an I commitment (one person can keep it alone) or a we commitment (it needs more than one party). Some are deliberately ambiguous; the explanation says why.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      A receiver who records only we lessons can hide his own errors inside the team’s. A receiver who records only I lessons leaves the relationship unchanged. Keeping both ledgers, separately and with owners and dates, is the simplest safeguard against both failures.

      A point of care

      The I ledger is personal and, in parts, private. A receiver should not be expected to write his most candid reflections into a document his client keeps. The repository record should hold the I commitments he chooses to share (what he will do differently), while his reasons and doubts stay in his own notebook. The we ledger is shared by design.

      Cards · I and we
      28 · From identified to learned

      Lessons identified are not lessons learned

      In brief

      NATO distinguishes a “lesson identified” (a problem observed, analysed and endorsed, with a remedy recommended) from a “lesson learned” (one that has been acted on and validated). The distinction exists because most lessons stop at the first stage. NATO’s own auditors found in 2017 that the majority of lessons identified from exercises were not sufficiently learned. Receivership reviews have the same problem, and the I/we split is part of the answer.

      NATO’s Joint Analysis and Lessons Learned Centre publishes a handbook, now in its fourth edition (2022), written to be relevant to any organisation. Its process runs from observation, through analysis and endorsement, to a lesson identified; then through a remedial action, its implementation and its validation, to a lesson learned. The US Army’s Center for Army Lessons Learned (CALL) performs the same function and was described by David Garvin as the Army’s institutional memory. A 2017 performance audit by NATO’s International Board of Auditors found that NATO commands were identifying lessons from exercises but that, because of shortfalls in reporting and incomplete implementation of remedial actions, few became lessons learned.

      The ARI researchers who reviewed Army practice in 2007 found something similar at the training centres: reviews of variable quality, often instructor-led despite the doctrine. Darling, Parry and Moore (2005) concluded that AARs often identify past mistakes but rarely improve future performance. The Army’s real secret, they argued, was not the review itself. It was the habit of carrying lessons forward, through a before-action review at the start of the next piece of work.

      Instrument 44 · The lessons pipelineWhere does each Ferrier House lesson stop?

      Each lesson from the review moves along the pipeline from observation to validation. Select a lesson to see how far it gets, what stopped it, and whether the I or the we ledger owns the next step. Then switch on “owner and date” to see what changes.

      Select a lesson.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      A lesson recorded in a closing report and never acted on is a lesson identified. It becomes a lesson learned only when the next appointment is run differently, and someone checks. That check is the first agenda item of the next before-action review.

      Cards · Lessons learned
      29 · Conditions

      Trust at the centre: psychological safety, blamelessness and a receiver’s accountability

      In brief

      “Trust / Commitment” sits at the centre of the xAAR diagram, and the research explains why. Teams learn when members believe it is safe to admit error. Learning-oriented reviews in software, wildfire and health have all moved away from blame. But a receiver is personally accountable in law, and a lender has commercial interests in the outcome. A receivership review must therefore be blameless about learning without pretending that accountability has gone away.

      Amy Edmondson’s 1999 study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company introduced team psychological safety: a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Psychological safety predicted learning behaviour, and learning behaviour in turn predicted performance. In a later and much-cited strand of her work she found that the better hospital teams appeared to report more errors, not because they made more, but because they were willing to talk about them.

      Google’s site reliability engineers made the same point for software. Their postmortem chapter says that for a postmortem to be truly blameless it must focus on the contributing causes of the incident without indicting any individual or team. The US Forest Service went further. Finding that its prescriptive model of accident investigation was not producing change, and developed first the Facilitated Learning Analysis and then the Learning Review, built around sensemaking rather than the attribution of cause. The Learning Review, introduced as part of a Coordinated Response Protocol, replaced the Serious Accident Investigation for the most serious incidents.

      Blameless, but not unaccountable

      A receivership review cannot simply adopt this. The receiver’s duties are personal and enforceable. The lender may have claims against a valuer or a monitoring surveyor. The borrower may later challenge the sale. A review whose records could be disclosed in litigation will not be candid. The practical answer has three parts. First, separate the forums: the joint review deals with the we ledger and with what each party is willing to commit to, while candid self-examination goes into the I notebook, which stays with its owner. Second, take advice on the status of the record where a claim is in prospect. Third, be clear in the room that the review is about learning and not about allocating liability, and that any question of liability will be dealt with elsewhere, by other means. The rule in good SRE practice applies: every action item has one named owner and a date. Blamelessness about causes is compatible with accountability for commitments.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      Without trust, the xAAR produces only the answers each party can safely give. The diagram puts trust and commitment at the centre for a reason: they are the condition of the review and its result.

      Cards · Conditions
      30 · Learning before doing

      Before the action: the premortem, the peer assist and the before-action review

      In brief

      Reflection-for-action has its own tools. In Gary Klein’s premortem, a team imagines that the project has already failed and works out why. A peer assist brings in people who have done similar work before. A before-action review restates what is supposed to happen and carries in the lessons from last time. For a receiver, all three belong in the first week.

      Klein described the premortem in the Harvard Business Review in September 2007. Team members assume that the project they are planning has just failed, then each writes down every reason he or she can think of. The method rests on research by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington (1989), who found that “prospective hindsight” (imagining that an event has already happened) increased people’s ability to identify reasons for future outcomes by about 30 per cent. Its practical virtue is permission: it lets people raise concerns they would otherwise keep to themselves for fear of seeming disloyal to the plan.

      Kahneman, who worked with Klein in what he called an adversarial collaboration, endorsed the premortem as one of the few debiasing tools that works in organisations. Their joint paper (2009) concluded that intuitive expertise is trustworthy only where the environment is regular enough to be learned and the practitioner has had adequate opportunity to learn it through feedback. That conclusion is important for receivers (section 34).

      Instrument 45 · A premortem for Ferrier HouseIt is twelve months from now and the appointment has failed. Why?

      Pick the reasons you think most likely. Each one, when chosen, shows how it would have shown itself early (the back-talk to watch for), the move that reduces it, and whether that move belongs to the I or the we ledger. The tally shows how many of your risks only a team can address.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      A premortem in week one costs an hour and surfaces the failure stories everyone half-knows. At Ferrier House most of the eventual surprises were on the list someone would have written.

      Cards · Before the action
      31 · Argyris and Schön

      Espoused theory, theory-in-use, and the two loops

      In brief

      Before he wrote The Reflective Practitioner, Schön worked for years with Chris Argyris. Together they distinguished what people say guides their action (espoused theory) from what actually does (theory-in-use), and single-loop learning (changing the action) from double-loop learning (changing the values and assumptions that govern it). Most AARs are single-loop. The I question becomes double-loop when it asks what the receiver assumed, not only what he did.

      In Theory in Practice (1974) and Organizational Learning (1978, revised 1996) Argyris and Schön argued that people hold two theories of action. The espoused theory is the one they give when asked. The theory-in-use is the one that can be inferred from what they do. The two often differ, and people are often unaware of it. Their most famous illustration is the thermostat. A thermostat that turns on the heat when the room is cold is single-loop: it detects an error and corrects it within a fixed setting. A thermostat that asked whether 18 degrees was the right setting would be double-loop.

      They described a dominant pattern of theory-in-use, which they called Model I. Its governing values are to achieve one’s intended purpose, to win and not lose, to suppress negative feelings, and to behave rationally. Its strategies are to control the task, protect oneself and others, and keep one’s reasoning private. Model I produces defensive routines and a win/lose world, and it blocks double-loop learning. Model II, the alternative, values valid information, free and informed choice and internal commitment, and asks people to make their reasoning public and test it. Schön devotes part of his town-planning chapter to a planner working in Model I, and shows how it limits what the planner can learn.

      Argyris’s best-known practical tool is the left-hand column. Write a difficult conversation on the right-hand side of the page, as it happened. In the left-hand column, write what you were thinking and did not say. The gap between the columns is where the theory-in-use shows itself.

      Instrument 46 · The left-hand column, and the two loopsWhat was said, what was thought, and what was assumed?

      This is the week-twenty-four call in which the contractor’s revised price arrived. Turn on the left-hand column to see what the receiver and the relationship manager were each thinking. Then choose a loop to see what each would have learned from it.

      Instrument 47 · The ladder of inferenceHow did a five-second observation become a belief about the agent?

      Argyris’s ladder, as popularised in Senge’s Fifth Discipline Fieldbook: a common mental pathway of increasing abstraction. Climb it rung by rung with the receiver’s call with the agent on day three. Then climb back down: at each rung, the reflective question that tests the leap. The reflexive loop on the left shows how the belief at the top changes what the receiver selects next time.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      A receiver’s espoused theory is in his proposals and reports: thorough, collaborative, value-maximising. His theory-in-use is in what he does on day one with a difficult agent at five o’clock on a Friday. The xAAR’s I question is the place to compare the two.

      Cards · Loops and models
      32 · The tradition

      The reflective tradition: Dewey, Kolb, Gibbs, Borton, Boud, Johns, Brookfield and Mezirow

      In brief

      Schön stands in a long line. John Dewey defined reflective thought in 1910. David Kolb drew the experiential learning cycle in 1984. Graham Gibbs turned it into a six-stage method in 1988. Terry Borton’s “What? So what? Now what?” became the simplest model of all. Boud, Keogh and Walker brought feelings back into reflection; Christopher Johns structured it for nurses; Stephen Brookfield gave it four lenses; and Jack Mezirow showed when it changes a person’s whole frame of reference. Each offers something specific to a receiver.

      Dewey’s How We Think (1910) defines reflective thought as active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief in the light of the grounds that support it and the conclusions to which it tends. It begins, he says, in a state of perplexity or doubt. That is Schön’s surprise, seventy years earlier. Kolb’s cycle runs from concrete experience to reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation, and back. Gibbs’s cycle, written for teachers, has six stages: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan. Borton (1970), adapted by Driscoll (1994) and by Rolfe, Freshwater and Jasper (2001), reduces it all to three questions.

      Boud, Keogh and Walker (1985) argued that the standard models neglected emotion. Their three stages are returning to the experience, attending to the feelings it evoked (using the positive and setting aside the obstructive), and re-evaluating it. Johns’s model of structured reflection, developed in nursing, asks a sequence of cue questions about aesthetics, personal knowing, ethics and empirics. Brookfield (1995) described critical reflection as checking the accuracy and validity of one’s assumptions through four lenses: one’s own autobiography, the eyes of those one serves, the eyes of colleagues, and theory and research. Mezirow’s transformative learning theory describes how a “disorienting dilemma” can lead, through self-examination and a critical assessment of assumptions, to a changed frame of reference.

      Instrument 48 · One event, eight modelsWhat does each model ask the receiver to notice?

      The event is day nine, when the fourth-floor tenant’s son was taken to hospital with an asthma attack and the receiver learned of it from a local newspaper’s website. Choose a model; the wheel redraws with its stages, and each stage shows the question it asks and the receiver’s answer.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      No single reflective model is right. Each makes the receiver notice something different, so the practical skill is choosing the model that fits the surprise.

      Cards · The tradition
      33 · The wider literature

      The literature mapped: three streams, a century of work

      In brief

      Reflective practice and the after action review grew up in separate worlds, and organisational learning and safety science in a third. The first stream runs from Dewey through Polanyi and Schön to critical reflexivity. The second runs from the Army’s training centres through medical simulation, software retrospectives and WHO’s action reviews. The third runs through Argyris, Weick, Nonaka, Edmondson and the just-culture movement. The xAAR sits where the three meet, and so does a receivership review.

      Stream one: reflection and the practitioner

      Dewey (1910) set the terms: reflection begins in perplexity and examines a belief’s grounds and consequences. Michael Polanyi supplied the epistemology Schön relied on. In The Tacit Dimension (1966) he wrote that “we can know more than we can tell”, and argued that formal knowledge rests on a much larger body of tacit knowing. Schön’s trilogy followed: The Reflective Practitioner (1983); Educating the Reflective Practitioner (1987), which asks what professional education would suit an epistemology of reflection-in-action and finds the answer in the studio, the conservatory and the coaching relationship; and, with Martin Rein, Frame Reflection (1994), which carries the idea of frames into intractable policy controversies, where appeals to facts fail and only reframing helps. In the 1987 book Schön describes three patterns of coaching: “follow me”, joint experimentation, and the “hall of mirrors”, in which coach and student each see their own practice reflected in the other’s.

      Later writers asked how deep reflection goes. Hatton and Smith (1995) distinguished descriptive writing, descriptive reflection, dialogic reflection and critical reflection; studies using their scheme commonly find that most written reflection by practitioners stays descriptive. Jennifer Moon’s handbooks (1999, 2004, 2006) gave reflective writing and learning journals a practical form, and Gillie Bolton’s Reflective Practice made writing itself a method of inquiry. Brookfield’s four lenses and Mezirow’s transformative learning (section 32) belong here. So does a critical turn: Ann Cunliffe’s “On becoming a critically reflexive practitioner” (2004) asked managers to examine how their own assumptions and actions shape the realities they then respond to. Thompson and Pascal (2012) argued for a more sociologically informed critically reflective practice that moves beyond Schön’s limitations. Reynolds and Vince’s Organizing Reflection (2004) moved attention from the individual reflective practitioner to collective and public reflection. Joseph Raelin’s “Public reflection as the basis of learning” (2001) argued that reflection becomes organisational only when it is done in the company of others.

      Stream two: reviews, debriefs and retrospectives

      The AAR (section 22) has cousins in every high-reliability field. Medical simulation built “debriefing with good judgment” at the Center for Medical Simulation in Cambridge, Massachusetts: Rudolph and colleagues (2006, 2007) drew directly on Argyris and Schön, treated the trainee’s mistakes as puzzles produced by frames, and paired advocacy (the instructor’s honest observation and judgement) with inquiry (genuine curiosity about the trainee’s reasoning). They called the approach “there is no such thing as non-judgmental debriefing”. Later blended models such as PEARLS combine plus/delta, advocacy-inquiry and directive coaching. Software developed the retrospective: Norm Kerth’s Project Retrospectives (2001) opened with a “prime directive” asking participants to believe that everyone did the best job they could given what they knew at the time, and Derby and Larsen’s Agile Retrospectives set out five stages: set the stage, gather data, generate insights, decide what to do, close. Google’s SRE practice, the Forest Service’s learning reviews, NATO’s lessons-learned process and WHO’s early, intra- and after action reviews complete the family.

      Stream three: organisations, sensemaking and safety

      Argyris and Schön’s organisational learning (section 31) is the trunk. Karl Weick’s sensemaking, defined as the ongoing retrospective development of plausible images that rationalise what people are doing, explains why every review is partly a story told after the fact, and why the first plausible story can foreclose inquiry. His question “how can I know what I think until I see what I say?” is a fair description of what a review does. Nonaka and Takeuchi’s SECI model (socialisation, externalisation, combination, internalisation) describes how tacit knowledge becomes organisational knowledge and back again. Edgar Schein’s Humble Inquiry (2013) describes the art of asking questions to which you do not know the answer. Edmondson’s psychological safety, Sidney Dekker’s just culture (a culture of trust, learning and accountability) and Erik Hollnagel’s Safety-II (learning from what goes right, not only from what goes wrong) supply the conditions.

      Where the streams meet

      Graves’s xAAR draws from all three without naming them. Its questions are the Army’s. Its I/we split restates the distinction between individual and organisational learning. Its repository is Nonaka’s externalisation and combination. Its centre, trust and commitment, is Edmondson and Dekker. A receivership review needs all three: the receiver’s own reflection, a disciplined team review, and an organisation (the lender) willing to learn.

      Instrument 49 · The literature mapWho said what, when, and what does it give a receiver?

      Eighty-seven works on a timeline from 1910 to 2026, in three streams. Select a work for what it contributes and how a receiver can use it. Filter by stream; the gold ring marks the works that feed the xAAR most directly.

      Select a work on the map.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      The literature runs in three streams that rarely meet. A receiver who takes something from each (a way of thinking, a review format and an organisational lens) has more to work with than any one tradition offers.

      Cards · The wider literature
      34 · When to trust the gut

      Intuition, feedback and the long cycle of a receivership

      In brief

      Kahneman and Klein agreed on two conditions for trustworthy intuition: an environment regular enough to learn, and adequate opportunity to learn it through feedback. Parts of a receiver’s work meet both conditions. Others, especially exit decisions, meet neither: the feedback (the sale price) comes months later and is confounded by the market. That is precisely where structured reflection is needed most.

      The 2009 paper “Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree” brought together a critic of intuition and its champion. Their conclusion was that judging the quality of an intuitive judgement requires asking how predictable the environment is and whether the person has had the opportunity to learn its regularities. Subjective confidence, they added, is not a reliable guide to accuracy.

      A receiver’s environment is mixed. His judgement on whether a building is being managed, formed in the first minute of a walk-round, is tested hundreds of times a career and corrected quickly: high validity, fast feedback. His judgement on whether to complete a part-built block is made a few times a career, with feedback a year later and confounded by a moving market: low validity, slow feedback. Schön’s banker could trust his gnawing feeling because he had felt it many times and seen what followed. A receiver should ask, each time he feels sure, which kind of judgement this is.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      Reflection-on-action shortens the feedback loop for decisions whose outcomes arrive late. Writing down, at the moment of decision, what one expects and why, and comparing it with the outcome months later, is the only way most receivers will ever learn whether their exit judgement is good.

      Instrument 50 · Where can a receiver trust his intuition?Validity of the environment, against speed of feedback

      Twelve recurring receivership judgements are plotted by how regular the environment is and how quickly feedback arrives. Select one for a reading and the reflective practice it calls for.

      Select a judgement.

      Cards · Intuition
      35 · Organisations

      The art of managing: how a lender learns, and the reflective contract

      In brief

      Schön’s eighth chapter argues that organisations have learning systems of their own, which tend to be “dynamically conservative”: they work hard to stay the same, and they treat surprise as a threat. A lender’s credit, recovery and panel functions are such a system. His last chapter proposes a “reflective contract” between professional and client, in which the client joins the inquiry instead of simply deferring to the expert. The xAAR’s we ledger is a reflective contract in miniature.

      Managers, Schön writes, reflect-in-action like other professionals, but they do so within an organisation whose learning system shapes what they can notice and say. Organisations are full of routines for avoiding surprise, and for keeping awkward information away from those who would have to act on it. Reflection-in-action that threatens the organisation’s stability tends to be suppressed. He describes managers who learn privately while the organisation learns nothing.

      In his final chapter he contrasts two contracts. In the traditional one, the client defers to the expert’s authority and the expert is expected to know. In the reflective contract, the professional acknowledges uncertainty, and the client agrees to join an inquiry, suspending disbelief instead of simply accepting authority. Each gains something. The client gains understanding and a share in the decisions; the professional gains information the client would otherwise withhold, and is released from pretending to know.

      A fixed charge receiver’s appointment begins under the traditional contract: the lender appoints an expert and expects certainty. Ferrier House shows the cost. The receiver’s first report, in week two, said more confidently than he felt that the upper floors could be completed for £1.4 million; the lender’s credit committee anchored on that number for five months. The xAAR at the end names it as a we lesson: the first report should state openly what is not yet known, and the lender should be willing to receive it that way.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      The receiver cannot make the lender a learning organisation. He can propose, in the first week, a reflective contract for the appointment: candid reports, review points, and a joint xAAR at the end. Most relationship managers welcome it.

      Cards · Organisations
      36 · The professional record

      Reflection in the profession: RICS CPD from 2026, and the receiver’s journal

      In brief

      Professional bodies now expect reflection, not just hours. From 1 January 2026, RICS members must still record at least 20 hours of CPD a year, at least 10 of them structured, but the revised framework asks members to plan their CPD, reflect on how it benefits their practice and record a learning outcome for each activity. A receiver’s I ledger is natural material for that record.

      The RICS rules effective from January 2026 require members to identify, plan, undertake and record CPD that is relevant, adequate and appropriate to their practice, with a minimum of 20 hours a year of which at least 10 must be structured. RICS describes the change as a move from tracking hours to focusing on how learning improves practice. Planning and reflection, and a recorded learning outcome for each activity, are now part of the framework. Members registered under the RICS and NARA Registered Property Receiver scheme have their own scheme obligations; reflection on appointments sits comfortably within both.

      Not every reflection is CPD, and a journal is not a substitute for structured learning. But a receiver who keeps an I ledger already has, at the end of each appointment, a candid record of what he learned and what he will do differently. Turning two or three entries a year into planned learning (a course on fire safety in part-converted buildings, say, after Ferrier House) closes the loop between reflection and development that the framework is now asking for.

      Check the current rules

      The summary above reflects the RICS framework effective from 2026 as published. Requirements change, and members should check the current RICS rules and guidance, and any scheme rules that apply to them, before relying on it.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      RICS’s new CPD rules make reflection a requirement. The opportunity is to make the required reflection the real one: the I ledger from an actual appointment, not a form filled in afterwards.

      Cards · Reflection in the profession
      37 · Putting it together

      The reflective receiver’s method: surface, map, test, review, pass on

      In brief

      Tacit knowledge, cognitive mapping and the extended After Action Review are not three separate subjects. They are three stages of one practice. The receiver surfaces what he knows tacitly (Critical Decision Method, left-hand column), maps it so it can be examined (cognitive and causal maps, repertory grid), tests it against the building (frame experiments, back-talk, a fuzzy map run forward), reviews it with the team (the xAAR, I and we kept apart), and passes on what can be passed on (externalised into the repository, socialised on walk-rounds, internalised in the next appointment). Each stage feeds the next, and the last feeds the first.

      The order matters. A review that begins without surfacing records only what people were already willing to say. A map drawn without surfacing captures the espoused theory, not the theory-in-use. A test without a map has no hypothesis to test. A review without tests repeats the first plausible story. And lessons that are reviewed but never passed on are, in NATO’s terms, identified and not learned.

      The I/we split runs through every stage. Surfacing is mostly individual: only the receiver can say what he noticed. Mapping is both: individual maps first, then a merged group map. Testing is mostly individual within the action-present and collective at the review points. Review is explicitly both, with two ledgers. Passing on is mostly collective: the repository, the protocol, the junior on the walk-round.

      Instrument 51 · The method, as a loopWhich tool, at which stage, for the I and for the we?

      The five stages form a loop around Schön’s two kinds of reflection. Select a stage for its tools, its Ferrier House example, what it produces for the I ledger and the we ledger, and how it fails if skipped. Toggle “Show the tacit layers” to see which kinds of tacit knowledge each stage can reach.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      The five stages are a checklist for any appointment. If the review feels thin, check which stage was skipped: usually surfacing, which leaves the review recording only what people were already willing to say.

      38 · The discipline

      A reflective practice for receivers: the day, the week, the appointment, the career

      In brief

      Reflection does not happen because a receiver believes in it. It happens because it has a place in the week. This section sets out a practice with four rhythms: a few minutes at the end of each day on site, a short weekly review, an AAR at each decision point and a joint xAAR at completion, and an annual look across appointments. Each rhythm has a different action-present and a different record.

      The day: thinking as you go

      On site, reflection-in-action needs one habit above all: noticing surprise and naming it, even silently. “That is not what the file said.” “She is more frightened than angry.” “The agent answered that too quickly.” Each named surprise is a candidate child session. At the end of the day, five minutes with the notebook: what surprised me, what did I do about it, which clock is it on?

      The week: the short review

      Once a week, before the lender’s report is written, the receiver runs the first three AAR questions privately for the week just gone: what was supposed to happen, what did happen, why the difference. He writes the I answer in the notebook and the we answer, if there is one, in the draft report. The report then says plainly what is known, what is not, and when it will be.

      The appointment: intra-action and after action

      At each major decision point (the end of the first fortnight, the complete-or-sell decision, the choice of buyer) the receiver proposes a short joint review with the relationship manager and the agent. These are intra-action reviews in the WHO sense: they can still change the appointment. At completion, the joint xAAR runs the five questions, fills both ledgers, and lodges the repository record with each party.

      The career: across appointments

      Once a year the receiver reads his I ledgers across all his appointments. Patterns appear that no single appointment would show: a recurring blind spot (fire safety in mixed-use buildings), a recurring strength (tenant communication), a repeated we failure with one lender. This is where double-loop learning happens for an individual practitioner, and where the CPD plan for the year should come from. It is also the best defence against over-learning that Schön describes.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      The four rhythms match the four widths of action-present a receiver works in. Each is short. Together they cost perhaps an hour a week, and they are the difference between thirty years of experience and one year of experience repeated thirty times.

      41 · The argument

      Objections, limits and replies

      In brief

      Reflective practice has serious critics, and so does the AAR. Schön’s concepts have been called vague; his “reflection-in-action” may describe something rarer than he claimed; reflection can be individualistic, uncritical, or a form of surveillance; and reviews can become ritual. This section sets out the strongest objections and the replies, and concedes where the objections win.

      “Reflection-in-action is mostly reflection-on-action in disguise.” This is Eraut’s objection, and it is partly right. Most of what receivers call thinking on their feet happens in pauses: in the car, overnight, between calls. But Schön’s action-present answers it. What makes reflection “in” action is not that it is instantaneous but that it still can change the outcome. On that definition, the receiver who rethinks the exit in month six is reflecting in action; the one who rethinks it in the closing report is not.

      “Schön’s concepts are too vague to use.” Critics including Eraut and later writers have said that terms such as frame, back-talk and repertoire are suggestive rather than precise. That is fair. This treatise has tried to make them usable by tying each to a concrete receivership move and a record. Vagueness at the level of theory is acceptable if the practice is specific.

      “Reflection is individualistic and ignores power.” Critics in education and social work have argued that reflective practice turns structural problems into personal ones, and can become a technology of self-surveillance. In receivership the risk is real: a receiver can write endless I lessons about problems that were caused by the lender’s instructions. The I/we split is part of the answer. So is Brookfield’s insistence on the lenses of others, and Mezirow’s on examining premises. Some problems belong to the we ledger, and some belong to neither, but to the market or the law.

      “AARs become a ritual.” Senge’s warning, and Darling and Parry’s, is that the review turns into a form to be completed. The evidence suggests the remedy: alignment with the real task, objective records, good facilitation, and a review of successes as well as failures. Above all, a lesson is not learned until the next appointment is run differently and someone checks.

      “Candour is dangerous where liability is possible.” Correct, and section 29 does not pretend otherwise. The answer is to separate forums and records, to take advice where a claim is in prospect, and to keep the shared ledger to commitments rather than confessions.

      “A receivership is too one-off for experiential learning.” Kahneman and Klein’s conditions are not met for exit decisions; feedback is slow and confounded. That is an argument for more structured reflection, not less: recording expectations at the moment of decision is the only way to learn from slow feedback at all.

      Why this matters for a receiver

      The objections are serious and some are unanswerable in principle. Taking them seriously keeps reflective practice honest: smaller claims, closer to the work, and open about its limits.

        Schön’s The Reflective Practitioner and Graves’s Five Elements method are paraphrased with short quotations and should be read in the original. The extended After Action Review is Tom Graves’s; the pentagon drawing of it was supplied by the author, and its receivership readings, including the emphasis on recording the I and the we as separate commitments, are this treatise’s own. The “lens reading” of the Five Elements is offered as a practical extension and is not attributed to Graves. Ferrier House, its people and its numbers are a composite for illustration. Effect sizes are reported as published and do not predict results in receivership. The summary of receivers’ duties and of RICS CPD rules is for orientation only and is not legal or regulatory advice. Principia Humanitatis · Mark Downham · 2026.
